notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1030.tmp1030.opp-lat: The text is badly scanned throughout; evident readings translated (e.g. 'Vas' = 'Nos', 'ronfitetur' = 'confitetur', 'ponimus id' = 'ponimus et', 'rara est' read as 'rata est', 'in duas ac simplices' = 'in duas simplices'). The sentence 'in qua re superatas difficultatis praemium vero, si...' is corrupt (a verb seems lost); rendered by sense with a bracketed supplement. The definition of the first sense of 'hypothesis' after Eudemus is garbled ('taleacqutrituraliquid... consentiendum') and translated by sense. In the Aristotle passage ('Idem cum sit et non sit... non necesse est esse b') the text appears defective: the argument (and the following lines) require 'it is not necessary that b not be', so a negation has been supplied in brackets.

Line 1: 'Cum sit igitur, b, non erit b' is evidently corrupt; translated as 'cum sit igitur a, erit b', which the argument requires. Later 'non erit Quia vero' lacks a letter, supplied as [b]. In the 'cor habere' example, 'quoniam tandiu...' is read as '[non] quoniam', required by the following 'sed'. Line 2: the third-figure example lacks an initial 'si', supplied. 'quolibet modo ex utrisque qui dicit, sunt, aut ea est negotio' is garbled; read as 'quolibet modo ex utrisque dicitur, [duae negationes] sunt, aut ea est negatio...'. 'quioque' read as 'quinque' (five). 'ante converso' read as 'an e converso'. In the first line, the enumeration 'contingere esse simpliciter, vel necesse esse dupliciter' does not yield the five modes the argument needs. The parallel passage later in the same line has 'necessarily in two ways, contingently in two ways', so the text here is probably corrupt; it is translated as printed. The clause 'quod si duarum inter se praedicativarum ... complexiones' is garbled and its syntax has been reconstructed loosely. The words 'etenim terminus applicatur' are obscure and have been rendered 'to whatever term it is applied'. Both 'Si Socrates sedet et vivit' and 'sol movetur, necessario venit' are read in the light of the argument: the first is taken as 'if Socrates sits, he also lives', and the second is a reconstruction of the misprint 'necessano verrit'. In the second line, the affirmative examples read 'si a non est, non est b' as printed, which duplicates the negative example; 'si non est a, est b' has been rendered, as the sense requires. In the same line, 'Neque enim propositionem esse ... cui non sentit auditor' is taken as reporting the opponents' view, with 'sentit' read as 'consentit'. Scanning errors corrected silently where evident (e.g. '£', '6', 'j6', '&', 'h' for b; 'sia' for 'si a'; 'ponendas' for 'ponenda'). In the second line 'vero prior propositionis pars auferatur' evidently lacks 'si'; supplied as [if]. In the same line 'secundum terminos ... necesse est si a fuerit, b non esse' is translated as it stands. In the first line, the clause 'Quod si cum non sit b, sit a, quod scilicet ex assumptione proponitur' is loose, since the assumption puts forward only that b is not; it is translated literally.

Several readings are evident scanning or edition slips, translated as intended: line 2 'n' for 'a'; in the second proposition of the long passage 'non est a' for 'non est c'; 'est q' (fifth) and 'est fi' (sixth) for 'est b'; in the fourth proposition the letter b is missing before 'inanimatum'. The eighth proposition's syllogism is printed 'cum sit b' but must be 'cum non sit b', as the proposition was given above. In the second proposition, 'cum b esse non possit' must mean that c cannot exist with b, and it is translated in that sense. In the third and fourth syllogisms the conclusions are printed 'non est c' and 'est c' respectively, which reverse their propositions; the sense requires 'est c' and 'non est c', and the bracketed renderings follow the sense.

The examples in lines 13–14 ("If a is man, when b is not animate…") do not fit the rule for these modes and seem corrupt; they are translated as printed. In the long final line the scanned text has several evident errors, translated as intended: 'psse/edse' = esse, '6', '!t', '£' = b, 'it' = a, 'repriebantur' = reperiebantur. In the example for the third proposition the text reads 'a animal, b animal'; the explanation that follows requires 'a animatum' (animate). In the third mode's second inference the text reads 'non est igitur a'; the sense requires c, and it is translated so. The closing list of examples is loosely punctuated in the edition; its parsing (e.g. the clause running 'si cum non sit a invitale, non est b, animal non est, c homo') is uncertain, and the words in brackets are supplied.

Line 35 is defective in the edition ("Si non est a, et si non est bf est c"); the missing "non est b" is supplied from the pattern of the series. In the second long line, the clause on the eight combinations in which the antecedent is removed says literally that they "preserve necessity in the same way"; the argument and examples require that they do not, so a negation has probably dropped out, and [do not] has been supplied.

The text is badly scanned and in places corrupt; evident readings have been translated. In the list of eight propositions, the last is printed 'si est b, non est c'; read 'si est a, non est c', as the scheme requires. 'hic igitur animal quod est, a non est; uno modo' is read as 'animal, quod est a, non uno modo'. In the second syllogism the edition prints 'si non est a, erit c', which contradicts the proposition ('if a is not, c is not'); translated as 'c will not be'. In the fifth syllogism the edition prints 'si igitur c, non est b', which contradicts the argument; translated as 'if c [is not], b is'. In the third syllogism, 'ea rerum est consequentia, ut si non sit c, sit a' is translated as printed. Other corrections were made silently: 'Sit' for 'Si' (fifth proposition), 'ratio' for 'ratus', 'item' for 'idem', 'ne animatum' for 'non amimatum'. The edition's 'vel etiam' and 'tantum' are rendered as 'and also' and 'on that account'.

Line 37: 'in aequimodas' ('inaequimodas') read as 'not in the same mode', as the sequel requires. Line 40 and 41: the lists of same-mode combinations are incomplete or disordered in the text and are translated as they stand. Line 43: 'Exponamus... in aequimodas propositiones' read as 'inaequimodas' (not in the same mode), as the examples show. 'Illic enim si c esset vel non esset' read as 'si a esset...', since in the second figure a is the shared antecedent. 'quo fit mortuum destruatur' seems corrupt; translated literally. In the third proposition 'si enim non sit, est b, est a' read as 'if b is not, a is'; in its example 'a animatum' must be 'a inanimatum', as the proposition shows. 'si non est animat' read as 'animal'.

The text has several evident scanning errors, corrected in translation: 'si non est & esta' read as 'si non est c, est a'; '£' read as b or c as the argument requires. In the eighth mode the printed text says 'I say that if b is not, c is not' (uon est c), but the argument and the following sentence ('if b is not, c will be') require 'c is'; the translation follows the printed words where they stand, and the reader should note the inconsistency. In the fifth mode, 'non esse' in 'perfecta conclusio non esse' is taken as 'that [b] is not'.

Many scanning errors in the long final passage (e.g. 'tl', 'cponatur', 'tfterminum', 'otermino', 'fuerilft', 'I!', '6' for a, c, d, b) have been read as the obvious letters. In the eighth proposition the letter 'a' is missing before 'animatum' and has been supplied in brackets. In the fifth proposition the text adds that b and d are such that if one is not, the other must be (sick/healthy as immediate contraries). The list of propositions where necessity arises 'in the fifth, seventh, thirteenth and fifteenth' is translated as printed.

The text is badly scanned and has several letter errors; these are read silently where evident. In the eleventh proposition, 'b sine b' is read as 'b sine d' and 'cum a negabitur' as 'cum c negabitur'. In the twelfth, 'Qvero' is read as 'a vero' and 'a nigrum' as 'd nigrum'; 'c negato, etiam negetur' lacks its subject, and d is supplied. In the twelfth example, 'Si tamen inanimatum homo sit' makes no sense as printed; it is read as 'si tamen non inanimatum homo sit'. In the sixteenth, 'praeter i:' is read as 'praeter c'. Several syllogisms as printed do not follow from their propositions, and the corrected readings are bracketed in the translation. These are the sixth, second form; the eighth, first form; and the fifteenth, second form. They look like printing errors. In the fifteenth, third form, 'est c' is read as 'est b'. The tally of forty conclusions does not add up as stated: 16+16+8. Of the four-fold propositions, it seems to count only the extra forms.

Line 72: 'v' read as 'c'. Lines 78 and 80: the text has 'cum sit c inanimatum' and 'cum sit c invitale', which do not fit the pattern of the examples (one would expect 'animatum' / 'vitale' or a negation); translated as printed. Line 84: 'modicus' read as 'medicus'. Line 85 has several corruptions: 'in collectibiles' read as 'incollectibiles' (yielding no inference); the repeated 'et si sit a, non erit b' read as 'si sit b, non erit a', as the sense requires; 'ut si vel non sit album' is garbled and rendered by sense as 'whether or not it is white'; 'id aut conjuncto quae disjunctiva ponitur' read as 'id "aut" conjunctio quae disjunctiva ponitur'. In the passage on 'either a is, or b is not', the clause 'in hac vero' refers back to the corresponding connected proposition, and is rendered accordingly.

nodes.text: TWO BOOKS ON THE HYPOTHETICAL SYLLOGISM BY ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS.
BOOK ONE.

While I consider that the highest comfort of life lies in learning and treating all the disciplines of philosophy, I take up with more pleasure, and as if with a certain reward even for the labour, the things I compose to share with you. For although the contemplation of truth is to be pursued for its own beauty, it becomes more lovable when it is brought out for common use. For there is no good that does not shine out more beautifully if it is approved by the knowledge of many. For what otherwise, held down by silence and on the very point of perishing in quietness, blossoms more widely and is defended from the death of oblivion by the sharing of those who know it, also becomes a more pleasant discipline, since it bids one be wise among those who share the same wisdom. And if it is added (as is now my case with you) that things pleasant in themselves are brought into the sharing of friendship, the sweetness of study must be seasoned, as it were, with the sweetest flavour of affection. For since friendship holds this as its proper office, that it does not want to have solitary thoughts, what anyone honourably thinks he confesses to no one more readily than to the one he loves. So it came about that, even if immense labour denied a way to the work begun, my mind was nevertheless equal to completing what it had undertaken through regard for you. For what great thing would my eager love for you achieve, if it had stopped within the bounds of ease? Therefore what I found among the Greek writers only in very few, and briefly and confusedly, but among the Latins in none, this our labour, though long, yet effective for what it began, has worked out and dedicated to your learning. For when you had acquired a very full knowledge of categorical syllogisms, you often asked about hypothetical syllogisms, on which nothing was written by Aristotle. Theophrastus, a man capable of every kind of learning, treats only the main heads of the matters. Eudemus walks a broader path of teaching, but in such a way that he seems to have scattered some seeds, as it were, yet to have brought forth no harvest of fruit. We therefore, so far as we were equal to it by the strength of our wit and by zeal for your friendship, have undertaken to clarify and to pursue carefully and precisely what was either said briefly by them or omitted entirely; and in this matter the reward of difficulty overcome [will be ample] if I seem to you to have fulfilled the duty of friendship, even if I do not seem to have satisfied [the demands of] learning. Every syllogism is contained in definite and suitably placed propositions. Every proposition is either categorical, which is called predicative, or hypothetical, which is called conditional. A predicative [proposition] is one in which one thing is predicated of another, in this way: a man is an animal; for here animal is predicated of man. A hypothetical [proposition] is one which declares with a certain condition that something is if something else is, as when we say thus: if it is day, there is light. Hypothetical propositions are made up of categorical ones, as will appear a little later; hence a syllogism composed of categorical propositions is called categorical, that is, predicative, while one that consists of hypothetical propositions is called hypothetical, that is, conditional. So, that the difference between these syllogisms may be seen clearly, their distinction in the nature of their propositions must first be examined; for in some propositions the predicative proposition seems to differ from the conditional in nothing except a certain manner of speech: as if someone proposes thus, a man is an animal, and again states it thus, if it is a man, it is an animal; these propositions are in a way different in speech, but they do not seem to have signified a different thing. First, then, it must be said that the predicative proposition establishes its force not in a condition but in predication alone, while in the conditional the ground of the consequence is taken from the condition. Again, the predicative is a simple proposition, while the conditional cannot be, unless it is joined from predicative propositions, as when we say: if it is day, there is light; it is day, and there is light, are two predicative, that is, simple, propositions. In addition, there is this, by which the property of each is most clearly shown: the predicative proposition has one term as subject and the other as predicate. And what is subjected in the predicative proposition seems to take on the name of what is predicated in the same proposition, in this way: when we say, a man is an animal, man is the subject, animal the predicate, and man takes on the name of animal, since man himself is proposed to be an animal. But in those propositions which are called conditional the manner of predication is not the same. For one is not predicated of the other at all; it is only said that the one is if the other is, as when we say: if she has given birth, she has lain with a man. For it is not then said that having given birth is itself the same as lying with a man, but only this is proposed, that a birth could never have been unless there had been intercourse with a man. And if ever the properties of both propositions meet in one and the same [proposition], then the way of understanding will vary according to the manner in which the proposition is stated, in this way. For when we say, a man is an animal, we make a predicative proposition; but if we propose thus, if it is a man, it is an animal, it is turned into a conditional statement. In the predicative, then, we shall look to this, that man himself is an animal, that is, takes on himself the name of animal. But in the conditional we understand this, that if there is some thing which is said to be a man, it is necessary that there be some thing which is called an animal. Thus the predicative proposition declares that the thing it makes subject takes on the name of the thing predicated. But the sense of the conditional proposition is this, that something is only if something else is, even if neither takes on the name of the other. So, the propositions having been distinguished by the property of their statements, syllogisms too have received their names, so that some are called predicative, others conditional. For those in which the propositions are predicative we call predicative syllogisms. But those in which the first proposition is hypothetical (for both the assumption and the conclusion can be predicative) are called hypothetical and conditional solely through the nature of the one hypothetical proposition. Now about the simple, that is, the predicative syllogisms, we have given an account in two little books which we composed on their construction. After the discussion of simple syllogisms, the order is that we discuss the non-simple. Non-simple syllogisms are those called hypothetical, which by a Latin name we call conditional. They are called non-simple because they consist of simple ones and are ultimately resolved into them, especially since their first propositions take the force of their own consequence from categorical, that is, simple, syllogisms; for the first proposition of a hypothetical syllogism, if it is doubted whether it is true, will be demonstrated by a predicative conclusion. The assumption too, in most modes of such syllogisms, is seen to be predicative, and likewise the conclusion, as when we say, if it is day, it is light; but it is day: this assumption is predicative, [and] if it is questioned, it will be proved by a predicative syllogism; it is light: therefore again a predicative conclusion has followed. Besides this, every conditional proposition is joined from predicative ones (as has been said). And if they both take their credibility from these and receive from them the order of their parts, categorical syllogisms must supply hypothetical ones with the force of their conclusion. But since we are speaking of hypotheticals, it must first be said what hypothesis means. For hypothesis, from which hypothetical syllogisms have received their name, is spoken of in two ways (as Eudemus holds): either something is granted through a certain condition agreed between [the parties] which could in no way happen, so that the argument may be brought to its end; or, a condition being laid down, a consequence is shown by force of conjunction or disjunction. An example of the former proposition is as if we were demonstrating that all corporeal things subsist by the concurrence of matter and form. For then we posit what cannot happen in the nature of things, and we separate the whole nature of form from the underlying matter, if not in reality, at least in thought; and since nothing of corporeal things remains, we consider it demonstrated and shown that the substance of corporeal things is made up of those same things by whose coming together it is formed and by whose separation and departure from each other it is destroyed. In this example, then, a condition of agreement having been laid down, so that what cannot happen is understood for a moment to happen, namely that forms are separated from matter, we look to what follows, namely that bodies perish, so as to prove that they consist of these same things. For since the destruction of corporeal things follows, we rightly say that all corporeal things consist of form and matter. But propositions of this kind, which arise from a condition agreed by the parties, differ in no way from the simple ones which the treatise of the first book of the Categorical Institution showed; those which do differ from the simple are these, when something is said to be or not to be, if something is or is not. These are always proposed with conjunctions, as when we say, if it is a man, it is an animal; if it is three, it is odd; or other things of this kind. For these are proposed in such a way that if any one thing is, another follows; or when we say, if it is a man, it is not a horse, here again it is proposed in the negative in the same way as above it was proposed in the affirmative; for here it is said, if this is, that is not; and the rest in this manner. They can also sometimes be stated in this way: when this is, that is, as when we say, when it is a man, it is an animal, or, when it is a man, it is not a horse; and this statement is of the same force as the proposition put thus: if it is a man, it is an animal; if it is a man, it is not a horse. Hypothetical propositions are also made by disjunction, thus: either this is or that is. Nor should this proposition seem the same as the one stated above thus: if this is, that is not. For that is not by disjunction but by negation. Every negation is indefinite, and therefore it can be used both of contraries, and of things intermediate between contraries, and of disparates. I call disparates those things which are merely different from each other, not in conflict by any contrariety, such as earth, garment, fire, and the rest. For if it is white, it is not black; if it is white, it is not red; if it is a branch of learning, it is not a man. But in the one made by disjunction one of the two must always hold, in this way: either day or night. And if we transfer to disjunction all those things which can properly be said by negation, the reasoning does not go through. For what if someone says, either it is white or black, either it is white or red, either it is a branch of learning or a man? For it can happen that it is none of these. Therefore, since the proposition by disjunction is laid down only in definite matters in which one of the two must occur, while separation by negation can be laid down in all things, even those which do not destroy each other's nature, they are distinguished by a clear principle. Every hypothetical proposition, then, is made either by connection (and I declare that the mode which is made by negation also belongs to connection) or by disjunction; for each mode is put together from simple propositions. Simple propositions are those we called predicative in the first book of the Categorical Institution. These are when something is predicated of something, either affirming or denying, as: it is day; there is light. But if a condition comes between them, it will become: if it is day, there is light; and one hypothetical proposition is made, joined from two categorical ones. But since every simple proposition is either affirmative or negative, hypothetical propositions can be made by connection in four ways: either from two affirmatives, or from two negatives, or from an affirmative and a negative, or from a negative and an affirmative. Examples of all of these must be given, so that what we are saying may become clearer. From two affirmatives: if it is day, there is light; from two negatives: if it is not an animal, it is not a man; from an affirmative and a negative: if it is day, it is not night; from a negative and an affirmative: if it is not day, it is night. But since it has been said that the same is signified by the conjunction 'if' and by 'when' when it is placed in hypothetical propositions, conditionals can be made in two ways: one according to accident, the other so that they have some consequence of nature. According to accident in this way, as when we say: when fire is hot, the heaven is round. For it is not because fire is hot that the heaven is round, but this proposition indicates that at the time when fire is hot, at the same time the heaven too is round. But there are others which have a consequence of nature to each other; of these too there is a twofold mode: one when it must follow, yet this consequence is not brought about by the placing of the terms; the other when the consequence is brought about by the placing of the terms. An example of the former mode is if we say thus: when it is a man, it is an animal; for this consequence rests on unshaken truth. But it is not an animal because it is a man; for the genus does not exist because the species exists, but perhaps the starting point is taken from the genus, and the cause of being can rather be drawn from universals, so that it is a man because it is an animal. For the genus is the cause of the species. Yet he who says, when it is a man, it is an animal, makes a correct and necessary consequence; but such a consequence does not proceed by the placing of the terms. There are other hypothetical propositions in which both a necessary consequence is found and the placing of the terms produces the cause of the consequence itself, in this way: if the earth comes in the way, an eclipse of the moon follows; for this consequence is valid, and an eclipse of the moon follows because the interposition of the earth comes between. These, then, are the propositions that are certain and useful for demonstration. We divide hypothetical propositions into two simple propositions, and the first, to which the conjunction is prefixed, we call the antecedent, the second the consequent; as in this one, if it is day, there is light, we call antecedent the part that says 'if it is day', and consequent the part 'there is light'. In disjunctive propositions, however, the order of statement makes the antecedent or consequent, as in: either it is day or it is night. For the one proposed first is called the antecedent, the later the consequent. And about the parts of hypothetical propositions this is enough. Now it seems we must explain what is also said by Aristotle: when the same thing is and is not, the same [consequent] need not be; as when a [is], b must for that reason be; [but] if the same a is not, it is not necessary that b [not] be because a is not. For the demonstration of a matter of this kind, the definition of the impossible must be set out first, which is this: the impossible is that which, once posited, commits [one to] something false and impossible on account of the fact that something impossible was posited at the outset. Let it be posited, then, that when a is, b is, that is, that there is such a consequence between a and b that, if it is granted that a is, it must be granted that b is. So let it be proposed: if a is, b is; I say that if a is not, it is not necessary that b be. And first let us consider what the consequence of the propositions is. For if the conjunction is such that if a is, b too must be, then if b is not, a too must not be; this is known from the following demonstration: if a is, b must be; I say that if b is not, a will not be. For let it be posited that b is not, and let a be, if that can be. But it was said that if a is, it must necessarily be granted that b is. Since, then, a is, b will be. For because we posit that b is not, b will not be; but because we posit that a is, b will be. Therefore b will both be and not be, which cannot happen. It is impossible, therefore, that b should not be and a should be. This is the firm demonstration we use. By an example it will become clearer: if there is a man, there is an animal; if there is not an animal, there is not a man. But it does not follow that if there is not a man, there is not an animal, for there are many animals which are not men. So in the consequence of a conjoined proposition, if the first is, the second must be; if the second is not, the first will not be. But if the first is not, it is not necessary that the second not be, nor indeed is it necessary that it be, for this is what we set out a while ago to demonstrate. For let a be, and when it is, let it be necessary that b be. I say that if a is not, it is not necessary that b be. I do not say that if a is not, it is necessary that b not be, but only that it is not necessary that b be. For since it was shown a little earlier that if b is not, a necessarily is not, then if it happens that this same term b is not, a will not be. But if, when a is not, it is necessary that b be, this same b will of necessity both be and not be. For because it happens that the term b is not, [b] will not be. But because if a is not, b will have to be, this same term b will both be and not be, which is impossible. From this, then, I consider it demonstrated that in a hypothetical proposition of consequence, if the first is, it follows that the second is; if the second is not, it follows that the first is not; but if the first is not, it does not follow either that the second is or that it is not. For this too is evident: if the second is, it does not follow either that the first is or that it is not; as in the proposition 'if there is a man, there is an animal', if there is an animal, it does not follow either that there is a man or that there is not; and if the first is not, it does not follow that the second necessarily is or is not, as in the same proposition, if there is not a man, it is not necessary either that there be an animal or that there not be. Of all these, then, only two consequences are stable and hold unchangeably: if the first is, that it follows that the second is; if the second is not, that it necessarily follows that the first is not. These things being settled, I shall add this: although no hypothetical proposition is simple, since it is conjoined from other propositions, there are nevertheless certain hypotheticals which, compared with other conditionals, would be judged simple. For every conditional proposition is either connected or disjoined; and since these are coupled from predicative [propositions], in connected propositions there must be four modes of this coupling. For a hypothetical proposition is either conjoined from two simple [propositions], and is called a simple hypothetical, like this: if a is, b is, as when we say, if there is a man, there is an animal; for 'there is a man' and 'there is an animal' are two simple propositions. Or it is coupled from two hypotheticals and is called composite, as when we say, if when a is, b is, then when c is, d is; as when we state it in a proposition such as this: if when there is a man there is an animal, then when there is a body there will be a substance. For 'if when there is a man there is an animal' is one hypothetical; the other is 'when there is a body there is a substance'; from these is conjoined one proposition which is called composite. Or it is coupled from one simple and one hypothetical, like this: if a is, then when b is, c is; as when we say, if there is a man, then when there is an animal, there is a substance. For 'there is a man' is a simple proposition; that when there is an animal there is a substance is shown to be hypothetical by the very consequence of the condition. Or it is put together from a hypothetical first and a simple [proposition] after, as when we say: if when a is, b is, c too will be; for example in this way: if when there is a man there is an animal, there is also a body. For the one which proposes 'if when there is a man there is an animal' is hypothetical; the later one which follows this hypothetical proposition, that is, 'there is a body', is simple. These too, since they are not coupled from simple [propositions], are called composite. Now the former, which consist of simple propositions and are called simple hypotheticals, are made up of two terms. By 'terms' I here mean the simple parts of a proposition from which it is joined. Of the composite hypotheticals, those which consist of two hypotheticals are coupled from four terms; but those which are conjoined from a hypothetical and a simple, or from a simple and a hypothetical, are conjoined from three terms. The differences and likenesses of these, then, the simple and the composite hypotheticals, must be stated. Those which are coupled from simple [propositions], if compared with those which are joined from two hypotheticals, have the same consequence, and the proportion remains; only the terms are doubled. For the place which the simple propositions themselves hold in hypothetical propositions consisting of simple ones, that same place is held, in propositions which are hypotheticals consisting of hypotheticals, by those conditions by which those propositions are said to be joined and coupled with each other. For in the proposition which says 'if a is, b is', and in the one which says 'if when a is, b is, then when c is, d is', the place which the earlier part, 'if a is', holds in the proposition contained from two simple [propositions], that same place is held, in the proposition coupled from two hypothetical propositions, by the earlier part, 'if when a is, b is'. For here the consequence is made by the condition of the conjunction of two propositions with each other. Likewise, the force which the following portion that is inferred, that is, 'b is', holds in a hypothetical coupled from two [simple] propositions, that same force is held, in the proposition joined from hypotheticals, by the part which follows, that is, 'when c is, d is'. And it differs only in this: in the first proposition, joined from simple ones, a proposition follows a proposition, while in the second, joined from hypotheticals, the condition of a consequence accompanies the consequence of a condition. For to say 'if a is, b is' is nothing other than [to say] that the proposition by which we say that a is has as its companion the one by which we predicate that b is; and in the proposition brought in from hypotheticals, when we say 'if when a is, b is, then when c is, d is', what is said is that the consequence which is between a and b has as its companion the consequence which is between c and d, so that if it follows that, a being posited, b is, it will without doubt follow that, c being posited, d is. But in propositions which consist of a simple and a hypothetical, the reasoning is that either the condition of a consequence follows a proposition, or the condition of a consequence accompanies what is proposed. For when we say 'if a is, then when b is, c is', we wish it to be understood that upon the proposition by which we say 'if a is' there follows the condition by which we say 'when b is, c is'; that is, that if a is, it is necessary that the term c be the companion of the term b. But when we say 'if when a is, b is, c is', we wish nothing else to be understood than that the truth of another proposition follows upon the consequence of two propositions with each other; so that if a and b have a consequence between them, it is necessary that the truth of the proposition by which we say that c is should follow this condition of consequence; that is, if it is necessary that, a being posited, b is, it is necessary also that c be. Similar syllogisms, then, will arise from those propositions which are joined from simple ones and from those which are joined from [components] both of which are not simple. But the syllogisms of those coupled from one simple and the other hypothetical turn out different from the former, yet similar to one another; nor does it matter for the modes of the syllogisms whether the first is hypothetical and the second simple, or conversely the first simple and the second hypothetical, except perhaps only for the interchange of the order itself. When, therefore, the reasoning of syllogisms has been demonstrated for those propositions which consist of simple ones, it seems to have been demonstrated also for those propositions which are put together from hypotheticals; and when the nature of the syllogisms of any of those propositions which consist of a simple and a hypothetical has been examined, it is shown also what sort of syllogisms the nature of the propositions with converted order produces. There is also another kind of propositions set in connection, which is in a way intermediate between those propositions joined from hypotheticals and simple ones and those coupled from two hypotheticals. For if you look to the number of terms, they consist as it were of three terms; and if you turn your mind to the conditionals, they seem to be composed as it were of two conditionals. This intermediate status comes about because one of their terms is found common to both conditionals. These are proposed either through the first figure, or through the second, or through the third. Through the first in this way: if a is, b is, and if b is, c is; thus b is counted in both, and the three terms are these: 'a is', 'b is', 'c is', while the two conditionals are these: 'if a is, b is', 'if b is, c is'; for b is common to both. And so propositions of this kind are intermediate between propositions composed from three terms and those composed from four. Through the second figure it is proposed in this way: if a is, b is; if a is not, c is. Through the third figure thus: [if] b is, a is; if c is, a is not. Let this suffice about connected [propositions]. Disjunctive propositions always consist of contraries, like this: either a is or b is; for when one is posited the other is removed, and when one is destroyed the other is posited. For if a is, b is not; if a is not, b is. In the same way also, if b is, a will not be; if b is not, a will be. These matters dispatched, let us return to connected [propositions]; for in them either a proposition follows a proposition, or a condition a condition, or a proposition a condition, or a condition a proposition. It must be said, then, which propositions appear to be consequents of which propositions, which differ as widely as possible from each other by way of contrariety, and which disagree by the contradiction of opposition. Of simple, that is, predicative propositions, some are proposed without a mode, others with a mode. Without a mode are all that signify pure being, in this way: 'it is day', 'Socrates is a philosopher', and those proposed similarly. Those with a mode are proposed thus: 'Socrates is truly a philosopher'; for here 'truly' is the mode of the proposition. But the greatest differences in syllogisms are made by propositions stated with a mode to which the word 'necessity' or 'possibility' is attached: of necessity in this way, when we say 'fire must be hot'; of possibility, as when we propose thus: 'it is possible for the Trojans to be overcome by the Greeks'. Hence every proposition signifies either that [something] belongs, or that it belongs necessarily, or, though something is not, nevertheless states that it can come about. Of these, the one which signifies belonging is simple and cannot be divided into any other parts. But the one which signifies that something belongs of necessity is spoken of in three ways: one in which it is like the proposition that signifies belonging, as when we say 'it is necessary that Socrates sit, while he is sitting'; for this has the same force as one who says 'Socrates sits'. Another signification of necessity is when we propose in this way: 'a man must have a heart while he exists and lives'; for this expression seems to signify, [not] that it is necessary for him to have it as long as he has it, but that it is necessary for him to have it as long as he who has it exists. Another signification of necessity is universal and proper, by which it predicates necessity absolutely, as when we say 'it is necessary that God be immortal', with no condition of limitation set against it. Likewise the possible is spoken of in three ways: either what is is said to be possible, as 'it is possible for Socrates to sit, while he sits'; or what can come about at any time while the thing remains to which something is proposed as able to come about, as 'it is possible for Socrates to read', for as long as Socrates exists he can read; again, that is possible which can come about absolutely at every time, as for a bird to fly. From this, then, it appears that some propositions signify belonging, others are necessary, others contingent and possible; and since the division of the necessary and the contingent is threefold, one from each of these divisions is referred to those that signify belonging. There remain, then, two necessary and two contingent, which, counted with the one signifying belonging, make five, all the differences of propositions. Of all these propositions, some are affirmative, others negative. The affirmative signifying belonging is the one which says 'Socrates is'; the negative, the one which proposes 'Socrates is not'. But of affirmative necessary propositions there appear to be two negations, one contrary, the other opposite. For of the one which says 'it is necessary that a be', in whichever of the two ways it is said, [the negations] are either the one which says 'it is necessary that a not be', or the one which says 'it is not necessary that a be'. Of these, the one which says 'it is necessary that a not be' is contrary to the one which says 'it is necessary that a be'; for both can be found false, as when we say 'it is necessary that Socrates read', 'it is necessary that Socrates not read': each is false. For when he reads, he does not read of necessity, and when he does not read, he is constrained by no necessity not to read; rather, either is possible. But the one which says 'it is not necessary that a be' is opposite to the one which proposes 'it is necessary that a be'; for one is always true, the other is always found false. In the contingent and the possible the reasoning is the same. For to the one which says 'it is contingent that a be' there seems to be set against it both the one which says 'it is contingent that a not be' and the one which proposes 'it is not contingent that a be'. The one which says 'it is contingent that a not be' is called a contingent negation, and can be true together with the affirmation which says 'it is contingent that a be', as when we say 'it is contingent that Socrates sit', 'it is contingent that Socrates not sit'. And these are not said to be contrary, since they can be true at the same time. But they are opposite whenever the contingent itself is negated, as when against the one which says 'it is contingent that a be' is set the one which says 'it is not contingent that a be'; for this signifies that it cannot be contingent at all. Since this is so, and since propositions signifying belonging are stated without any mode, in them a full negation is made by joining the negative adverb to 'to be'. But with those which are put forward with a mode, if they are necessary and the negation is joined to 'to be', as in the one which says 'it is necessary not to be', the result is a necessary negation. But if the negation is placed before the 'necessary' itself, the result is a negation of the necessary, strongly opposed to the affirmation, as in the one which says 'it is not necessary to be'. Likewise in contingents, if the negation is placed before 'to be', the result is a contingent negation, as in the one which says 'it is contingent that a not be'. But if the negation is joined to the 'contingent' itself, the result is a negation of the contingent, strongly opposed to the contingent affirmation, as in the one which says 'it is not contingent to be'. But every proposition is put forward as universal, particular, indefinite or singular: universal in this way, 'Every man reads'; particular thus, 'Some man reads'; singular thus, 'Socrates reads'; indefinite thus, 'Man reads'. So it is necessary, as was shown in the Institution of Categorical Syllogisms, that those propositions seem most opposed to one another which either affirm universally while it is denied particularly, or deny universally while it is affirmed particularly, and, among singulars, where one is placed in affirmation and the other in negation. Since this is so, if this same reasoning is applied to contingent and necessary propositions, the same is found in necessary and contingent ones. So if someone says 'it is necessary that every term a be', and another denies it, saying 'it is not necessary that every term a be', he has made the opposite negation. And if someone says 'it is contingent that every term a be', and someone denies it, 'it is not contingent that every term a be', he has made the opposite negation; for in both cases the negation both removes the mode and cancels the signification of universality. This must indeed happen in simple and categorical propositions, whose nature we have treated more carefully in the volumes which we entitled the exposition, in the second edition, of the Peri hermeneias. If, then, someone should inquire into the number of all conditional propositions, he will be able to find it from what [is found] in categoricals. It is to be sought first in connected propositions made from two simple ones, in this way. Since a simple hypothetical proposition is joined from two categoricals, one of them will signify either belonging, or being contingent simply, or being necessary in two ways; if they are affirmative, they are put forward in five ways by an affirmative statement. But since every affirmation has an opposite negation, a negative statement can again be uttered in five ways. In the first proposition, then, which is one part of the hypothetical proposition, there will be ten propositions of the modes, made up of negation and affirmation. The second proposition too, which is part of the hypothetical, can be put forward with as many affirmations and negations; so it too will have ten statements. But since the first proposition is coupled to the second by a certain consequence, so that one hypothetical results, all ten affirmative and negative propositions will be applied to all ten affirmative and negative propositions. So, combined, they produce a hundred propositions in all, those which are joined as connected propositions from simple ones. By this method the number of propositions can also be found in propositions coupled from a categorical and a hypothetical, or made from two conditionals. For those which consist of a conditional and a categorical, or which, put the other way, are joined from three categoricals: if the combination of two predicatives with each other, in affirmation or negation, [signifying] either being, or being necessarily or contingently, in five modes produces a hundred combinations, [then,] since the third proposition will be affirmative or negative, and if affirmative, in five modes (either signifying belonging, or belonging necessarily in two ways, or belonging contingently in two ways), and will likewise be denied in as many modes, it will be stated in all no more than ten times. Hence the third proposition, joined and linked with the two above, which are coupled and combined with each other in a hundred modes, makes a thousand combinations in all. For the hundred modes of the two propositions, combined with the ten modes of the third proposition, make a thousand: ten times a hundred is a thousand. Again, since a conditional joined from two hypotheticals is coupled from four categoricals, and the first two categoricals were joined with each other in a hundred combinations, the latter two must also be connected in a hundred combinations; and if the hundred modes of the former categorical propositions are combined with the hundred modes of the latter categoricals, there will be ten thousand combinations. But in those propositions which vary in three figures, if the middle term is put forward in the same way in both the first and the second hypothetical, there will be a thousand combinations, like those connected from three categoricals; for then one and the same term in both will make three statements and no more. It is put forward in the same way in both like this: 'if a is, b is; if b is, c is'; for here the term b is placed both with respect to the term a and to c, signifying belonging. The same is to be understood in necessary and contingent ones. But if it is put forward thus: 'if a is, b is, and if it is necessary that b be, c is or is not', the result is two conditional propositions, that is, four predicatives. Hence, like those connected from four predicatives, they make ten thousand combinations; and these numbers are to be examined in the first as well as in the second or third figure. We have set down how great the number of propositions could be; yet the middle term is never stated dissimilarly. For in order that a conclusion of the extremes may come about, the middle term comes between, and what it shares joins the extremes. But if the middle is stated in different modes in each proposition, the extremes are not connected, and therefore no syllogism at all can come about, especially since not even a single proposition can be stated in which the middle term is stated dissimilarly. The number of propositions would be far more manifold if we were to vary the affirmative and negative propositions signifying belonging, the necessary and the contingent, through universals and particulars, whether opposite or subalternate. But this is not fitting, because the terms of conditional propositions are for the most part stated in an indefinite mode. And therefore I judged it superfluous to seek out the multitude of propositions determined according to quantity, since conditionals are not usually put forward determinately. Generally, indeed, hypothetical propositions are not even stated through necessity or through the contingent; rather, those which signify belonging are mostly brought into the use of speech. But all of them are meant to hold a necessary consequence: those which signify belonging, those to which necessity is added, and those to which the predication of possibility is fitted, to whatever term it is applied. The necessity of a hypothetical proposition, and the reasoning of the propositions from which connections are joined together, looks to the consequence. For example, when I say 'if Socrates sits, he also lives', it is necessary neither that he sit nor that he live; but if he sits, it is necessary that he live. Likewise, when we say 'the sun moves, it necessarily comes to its setting', this signifies just as much as 'if the sun moves, it comes to its setting'. For the necessity of the proposition consists in the immutability of the consequence. Likewise, when we say 'if it is possible for the book to be read, it is possible to reach the third line', the necessity of the consequence is again preserved; for if it is possible for the book to be read, it is necessary that it be possible for the third line to be reached. Only those propositions are opposed to hypothetical propositions which destroy their substance. The substance of hypothetical propositions lies in this, that the necessity of their consequence is able to remain. So if someone is to contradict a conditional proposition correctly, he will do it by destroying its consequence. For example, when we say 'if a is, b is', he will not contradict it by showing either that a is not or that b is not, but by showing that, a being posited, it does not at once follow that b is, but that a can be even if the term b is not; and if it is a negation, the conditional will be destroyed in the same way, as when we say 'if a is, b is not'. It is not to be shown either that a is not or that b is, but that while a is, the term b can be. Some hypothetical propositions are affirmative, others negative. I am speaking now of those which, being placed in a consequence, are said to be in connection. Affirmative, as when we say 'if a is, b is', 'if a is not, b is'; negative, 'if a is, b is not', 'if a is not, b is not'. For one must look to the consequent proposition to judge whether the proposition is affirmative or negative. The same will need to be understood of composite conditional propositions. Of the propositions placed in disjunction I shall speak more conveniently and fully when I treat their syllogisms. Hypothetical syllogisms, which in Latin we call conditional, are thought by some to consist of five parts, by others of four, by others of three. I shall soon decide their dispute, once I have first shown by what names the parts of such syllogisms are called. Since every syllogism is woven from propositions, the first is called either the proposition or the premise taken; the second is called the assumption; and what is inferred from these is called the conclusion. When we say 'if it is a man, it is an animal; but it is a man; therefore it is an animal', the statement by which we say 'if it is a man, it is an animal' is called the proposition or premise taken; the one we have added to it, 'but it is a man', is called the assumption; the third is named the conclusion, by which we show that what was a man is an animal. But since it often happens that the consequence of the propositions stated is not plausible, a confirmation is often added to the proposition, by which what was proposed may be shown to be true. Since the assumption too often does not seem fit for belief by itself, the aid of a proof is added to it as well, so that it may seem true. Hence it happens that hypothetical syllogisms often have five parts, often four, sometimes three. A syllogism will consist of five parts if both the proposition and the assumption need proofs; if either the proposition or the assumption needs a proof, the syllogism is four-part; and if neither is to be confirmed, it remains that it is three-part. Marcus Tullius too is found to hold this view: in the Rhetorical books he affirms that some syllogisms are five-part and others four-part. Those, however, who do not accept that the parts of such syllogisms extend beyond the number three, think that the proofs of propositions and of assumptions are not to be counted among the parts of the syllogism. For [they say] a proposition to which the hearer does not assent is not one from which a syllogism can arise. If the proposition is doubtful by itself, the proof which is added to the doubtful proposition, by creating belief in the very proposition to which it is added, makes it fit for a syllogism; and so it begins to be a proposition of the syllogism only when it is made such by the proof that something can be inferred from it; and something can be inferred from it only when, with the help of the proof, it can be granted by the hearer. Therefore the proof of a doubtful proposition or assumption seems to be a member of it and, as it were, a prop, not also a part of the syllogism. Our own view inclines rather to those who declare that it consists of three parts. For any proof which is coupled to a proposition or an assumption is called the proof of the proposition or of the assumption. Since, then, it is referred not to the syllogism but to the proposition or assumption whose proof it is, it ought not to be regarded properly as a part of the syllogism. As for the objection that can be raised, no one is unaware that the parts of parts are also said to be parts of the whole. But it makes a very great difference whether they are themselves parts of the whole in the first place, or are placed at the far end, among secondary parts. Further, if the proposition is plausible and known by itself, the whole syllogism needs no proof. But if the proposition has no credibility by itself, that proposition must need the proof as a kind of testimony. So it is not the syllogism, insofar as it is a syllogism, that will need a proof, but the proposition, if it lacks credibility of its own. The same can be said of the assumption. It is therefore clear that the view which asserts that a syllogism is joined from three parts only is to be preferred. Moreover, if some proposition needs a proof so that true belief may follow it, it will be demonstrated by some syllogism. How then can a syllogism rightly be called part of a simple syllogism? For the proof of a proposition must itself be a syllogism or come from a syllogism. With these points settled, it seems we must next explain those syllogisms whose propositions, placed in connection, consist of two terms. They have a twofold form: four come about through the affirmation of the antecedent proposition, and these are the first and perfect hypotheticals; and four through the negation of the consequent, which, since they need demonstration, do not seem to be perfect. By negating the antecedent and positing the consequent no syllogism at all is produced. First, then, let the number of all such propositions be set out, so that the syllogisms which come from them may be easily recognised. There are four: 'if a is, b is'; 'if a is, b is not'; 'if a is not, b is'; 'if a is not, b is not'. We must speak first of the earlier and perfect syllogisms. The first mode of these is this one, coming from the first proposition: 'if a is, b is; but a is; therefore b is'. Since the first proposition puts forward only the condition that if a is, the being of the term b must necessarily follow, the assumption takes and posits the antecedent and says 'but a is'; it follows therefore that b is, for this is brought about by the consequence of the first proposition. But if we posit the consequent by assuming it, no syllogism results. Let there be a consequence of this kind: 'if a is, b is', and let the consequent be assumed thus: 'but b is'; it does not follow either that a is or that it is not. This will become clearer by an example. Let the proposition be 'if it is a man, it is an animal', and let it be assumed that it is an animal, that is, the consequent; it will not be necessary either that it be a man or that it not be, for when it is an animal it can be this or not be this. The second mode is of those in which the first part of the proposition is repeated in the assumption. It comes from the second proposition set out above, thus: 'if a is, b is not; but a is; therefore b is not'; for it had been proposed that if a were, b would not be. So when the antecedent is taken, the conclusion of the consequent is made; but if you take the consequent, no syllogism seems to come about, because no necessity follows, thus: 'if a is, b is not; but b is not'; it is not necessary that a be, or that it not be. Let the proposition be 'if it is black, it is not white', and let the consequent be assumed: 'but it is not white'; it will not be necessary that it be black or that it not be, because when it is not white, it can be something intermediate. The third mode of such syllogisms is the one which comes from the third proposition, in whose assumption the antecedent is posited, thus: 'if a is not, b is; but a is not; therefore b is'; therefore this conclusion again comes about from the condition of the proposition, for it had been proposed that if a were not, b would be. But if you convert it and take that b is, that is, the consequent, it will not be necessary that the antecedent be or not be. But no example of this can be found, because if it is proposed in such a way that when a is not, b is, there seems to be nothing intermediate between a and b. In these, if one of them is not, it is at once necessary that the other be, and if one of them is, it is at once necessary that the other not be. So in these a syllogism seems in a way to come about when the consequent is posited. But this holds as regards the nature of the thing; as regards the condition of the proposition itself, it does not follow at all. This is clear from what was said above. For in both the modes above, when the consequent was posited, nothing was gathered of necessity. And this third mode, as regards the combination of the propositions, produces no syllogism if what followed is assumed by positing it. But as regards the nature of the things, in which alone these propositions can be stated, the consequence seems to be necessary, thus: if it is not day, it is night; if it is night, it follows of necessity that it is not day. These syllogisms are like those constituted in disjunction, which I shall mention a little later, and I shall give both the differences and the likenesses of these to those. The fourth mode comes from the fourth proposition, when it is proposed thus: 'if a is not, b is not; but a is not; therefore b is not'. For again this too is shown to follow from the proposition, which proposed that b would not be if a, the first term, were not. But if we assume the consequent, no necessity seems able to come about; for example, if we say 'but b is not', it will not be necessary that a be or not be. Let it be proposed: 'if it is not an animal, it is not a man', and let it be assumed: 'but it is not a man'; it is not necessary either that it be or that it not be an animal. It has therefore been shown that in syllogisms of this kind, if the antecedent is assumed by positing it, the syllogisms that come about are perfect, acceptable from the propositions themselves, and necessary; but if the consequent is assumed by positing it, no necessity comes about, except in the third mode. Since that mode is like the syllogisms which come about through propositions stated by disjunction, it seems to preserve necessity in the things about which it can be proposed, although it does not preserve it in the combination. This is shown from the other three modes, the first, second and fourth, in which, when the following part of the proposition is taken by positing it, nothing is concluded of necessity. And we have said enough about those syllogisms which are joined by two terms, in which the first part of the proposition is assumed by positing it, as far as the manner of instruction requires. Now we must speak of those in which the consequent of the proposition is taken so as to be destroyed. From these too four modes come about, since the first part of the proposition cannot be destroyed in the assumption in such a way that any necessity of syllogism follows. The first mode of such syllogisms, then, comes from the first proposition, thus: 'if a is, b is; but b is not; therefore a is not'. Here the term b, which had been the consequent in the first proposition, is destroyed in the assumption, so that the term a, which had been the first part of the proposition, is destroyed. This necessity will be proved by the following reasoning. For it was proposed that if a is, b is; and the assumption was made so as to destroy the consequent part of the proposition, that is, that b is not. I say that it follows that a is not. For if a can be when b is not, the first proposition, which says that if a is, b is, will be idle. But that proposition holds; therefore when a is, b is. But if a is when b is not, which is what the assumption puts forward, the same b will both be and not be: it will not be, because the assumption puts forward that b is not; and it will be, because if a is, b will be; and this cannot happen. Therefore a will not be if b is not. This, then, is the first mode of such syllogisms, which come about from the destroyed consequent part of the proposition. They are not perfect, nor known through themselves, but need either the proof I set out above or some other proof to be shown true. But if the first [part] of the proposition is destroyed, there will be no syllogism. Let us say: 'if a is, b is; but a is not'; it does not follow that b either is or is not, as is also shown by an example. Let the proposition be: 'if it is a man, it is an animal; but it is not a man'; it will not be necessary either that it be an animal or that it not be. The second mode by contradiction in the assumption, which descends from the second proposition, is when we propose thus: 'if a is, b is not; but b is; therefore a is not'. For here again the second part of the proposition is destroyed: for whereas the second part of the proposition said that b is not if a were, the assumption declares that b is. And the affirmation destroys the negation, through which assumption it follows that a is not, in this way. Let the proposition be 'if a is, b is not', and let b be. I say that a will not be. For if a is, while b is, the same b will both be and not be: it will not be from the first proposition, which says 'if a is, b is not'; and it will be through the assumption, by which we say that b is. But if the antecedent part of the proposition is removed, no necessity will come about. Let us say in a proposition of this kind, 'if a is, b is not': 'but a is not'; it does not follow that b either is or is not. This is shown by the following example. Let us say 'if it is black, it is not white', and let us assume that it is not black; it does not at once follow that it either is or is not white, for it can be something intermediate. The third mode is the one derived from the third proposition, when we propose thus: 'if a is not, b is; but b is not; therefore a is'. Here too the consequent part of the proposition is assumed, and whereas it was affirmed in the proposition, it is denied in the assumption; and the consequence is valid and completes the syllogism, in this way. For if it is true that when a is not, b is, I say that if b is not, a is. For if a can not be when b is not, the first proposition, which says that when a is not, b is, is idle; and b will both be and not be: it will not be from the assumption which puts forward that b is not; and it will be because, if the term a is denied to be, then, with the term b posited as not being, since a is not, b will be; which is impossible. Therefore it cannot happen that when b is not, a is not. It follows, then, that when b is not, a is. But if the first part of the proposition, which is the antecedent, is removed, there is no syllogism, in this way: For when we say 'if a is not, b is', if we assume 'but a is', nothing necessary results, so that b either is or is not, according to the nature of the combination itself. For here too, as in those in which the second term was posited in the assumption, it must be said that according to the nature of the combination itself no syllogism comes about; but according to the terms, in which alone it can be said, it is necessary that if a is, b is not. For only in contraries, and in those that are immediate, that is, that have no intermediate, can this proposition truly be predicated, as when we say 'if it is not day, it is night': whether it is not day, it will be night; or it is not night, it will be day; or it is day, it will not be night; or it is night, it will not be day. The fourth mode of these syllogisms descends from the fourth proposition, whose first proposition is this: 'if a is not, b is not; but b is; therefore a will be'. Here too the second part of the proposition is assumed, and since it had been posited with a negation, it is destroyed by an affirmation; for the affirmation destroys the force of the negation. Here too the necessity of the syllogism is maintained in the same way. For if, it being posited that when a is not, b is not, it is taken that b is, I say that it follows also that a is. For if a can not be when b is, the first proposition, which declares that when a is not, b is not, is idle; so again it will come about that the same b both is and is not. For from the assumption b will be, since it is said 'but b is'. But if, this being posited, a could not be, then again b will not be, because the first proposition says 'if a is not, b is not'; which is impossible. But if the portion of the proposition which is the antecedent is removed, nothing necessary results. Let us say 'if a is not, b is not', and let us assume 'but a is'; it does not follow that b is necessarily concluded either to be or not to be, as in this syllogism: 'if it is not an animal, it is not a man; but it is an animal'; it is not necessary either that it be a man or that it not be. These four syllogisms, then, are called imperfect, because they do not have of themselves an open and evident necessity of consequence, and it is produced for them by proof. So, to conclude briefly: in simple hypothetical syllogisms having connected propositions, however made, if the first part of the proposition is assumed, and it is posited, four syllogisms will come about that are known through themselves and perfect; but if the consequent is assumed, no syllogism has necessity, except only in the third, which seems to hold the necessity of the conclusion not because of the nature of the combination, but because of the contrariety of the terms in which alone it can be said. So, if something of what was stated in the proposition is posited in the assumption, it is necessary that four or five perfect syllogisms come about: four where the first part of the proposition is assumed by positing it, five where the second part is, if we look not to the nature of the combination but to the terms. But if something of what the first proposition states is removed in the assumption: if it is the consequent part of the proposition that is removed, four syllogisms will come about that are imperfect and need proof; [if] the first part of the proposition is removed, there will be no necessity of syllogism, except only in the third mode, where it is not the combination that produces necessity but the nature of the terms. Therefore here too there are four or five syllogisms: four if the second part of the proposition is destroyed, and a fifth if it is measured not by the nature of the combination but by the property of the terms. Therefore, if the first proposition consists of two terms, there are eight or ten syllogisms, and no more. And enough has been set out about those conditional syllogisms whose propositions are connected and consist of two simple predicative [propositions]. Now we must speak of those syllogisms which are connected from a predicative and a hypothetical, or from a hypothetical and a predicative. The combinations of all these syllogisms will easily appear if their number is first set out. The first, then, those connected from a predicative and a hypothetical, are these:
If a is, when b is, c is.
If a is, when b is, c is not.
If a is, when b is not, c is.
If a is, when b is not, c is not.
If a is not, when b is, c is.
If a is not, when b is, c is not.
If a is not, when b is not, c is.
If a is not, when b is not, c is not.

And first it seems we must treat what their nature is. For a conditional proposition will not result from positing a condition in just any way, but only if the consequence comes about on account of the condition posited. For if someone says, 'if it is a man, when it is an animal, it is animate', the added condition does not seem to produce the necessity of the consequence; for even if it is not a man, still, when it is an animal, it is animate. But if it is put thus, 'if it is a man, when it is animate, it is an animal', the ground of the consequence seems to rest on the condition. For it is not necessary that when something is animate it is an animal, unless what is proposed as animate is a man or some such thing. For then what is animate must be an animal, since a man, or anything else of that kind, is animate. We must therefore go through the propositions one by one and examine the nature of each, in this way. The first proposition, by which it is stated 'if a is, when b is, c is', must be such that b can indeed exist even apart from a, yet if a is, b cannot fail to be. Again, the same term b can exist even when c is not, and it is not necessary that when b is posited c also is; but it is necessary that c is only when the term b follows the term a. For example, let a be man, b animate, c animal: animate can exist both apart from man and apart from animal. But if it is a man, it must be animate; and since animate follows the essence of man, it follows in that case that the animate thing is an animal. Likewise the second proposition, which says 'if a is, when b is, c is not', will have to be such that b can exist apart from a, but when a is, b must also be. And c must be such that it cannot exist together with a, but can both exist and not exist with b; but it is only when the term b follows the term a that [c] cannot exist with b. For example, let a be man, b animate, c insentient. For animate can exist apart from man; but if it is a man it must be animate; and an insentient thing can be animate and can also not be. But insentient and animate do not go together when something is animate because it was stated beforehand to be a man. The third proposition must have a term a which can never exist together with the term b; and the term c will have to be such that it can both be and not be if b is not, but it is necessary that the term c is when the term b is not only if b is not because the term a was stated beforehand to be. For example, let a be man, b inanimate, c sentient. For if it is a man, it is not inanimate; but sentient can both be and not be when [something] is not inanimate. For there can be some things which are neither inanimate nor sentient, such as trees. Yet it is necessary that the same thing is sentient when it is not inanimate, if it is not inanimate because it was stated beforehand to be a man. Again, the fourth proposition must have this property: that the term b can in no way exist if a is, while c can both be and not be if b is not. But c must fail to be when b is not only if the term b is not because the term a was proposed beforehand to be. For example, let a be man, [b] inanimate, c insentient: for it will not be inanimate if it is a man; and insentient can both be and not be if it is not inanimate. It is necessary that it is not insentient when it is not inanimate only when it is not inanimate because it was stated beforehand to be a man. The fifth proposition too must have such terms that if a is not, b must be; and if the term b is, c can both be and not be. It is necessary that c is when b is only when b is because the term a was denied to be. For example, let a be animate, b insentient, c lifeless. So if it is not animate, it follows at once that it is insentient; and it can be lifeless if it is insentient, like a stone, but it can also not be lifeless if it is insentient, as trees are. But only then, when insentient is posited, does it follow that it must be lifeless, when it is insentient because it is not animate. The sixth proposition requires such terms that b must be if a is not, while the term c, if b is, can either be or not be; yet c must fail to be when b is, when b is because the term a was proposed not to be. For example, let a be animate, b insentient, c living. For it must be insentient if it is not animate; but when it is insentient, it can happen that it does not live, like a stone, and it can happen that it lives, like a tree; yet it is necessary that it does not live, when it is insentient, when it is insentient because it was proposed not to be animate. The seventh mode must be constructed with such terms that b cannot exist without a, while if c is not, b can both be and not be; yet the term c must be if b is not, when b was posited not to be because a had been denied. For let a be animate, b sentient, c lifeless. Now a thing cannot be sentient unless it is animate. So if it is not animate, it will not be sentient; but if it is not sentient, it can be lifeless, as in stones, and it can also not be [lifeless], as in trees; yet when sentient is denied, it must be lifeless, when it is not sentient because it was posited not to be animate. The eighth proposition must be joined from these terms: that the term b cannot be if a is not, while when b is not, the term c can both not be and be. But the term c must not be when b is not, when b is not because the term a was previously denied to be. For example, let a be animate, b sentient, c living. A thing cannot be sentient unless it is animate; yet if it is not sentient, it can both be and not be living — not be, like stones; be living, like trees; yet it is necessary that it is not living, if it is not sentient, when it is not sentient because it was previously denied to be animate. From these, then, it is clear that the term c, in whatever way b stands, in the conditional propositions which are placed after the predicative ones in the whole statement, can be assumed in the place either of an affirmation or of a negation; and from these assumptions come the various combinations of syllogisms. These matters being thus set out, it seems we should give rules about all of them in common. For since there are eight propositions joined from a predicative and a hypothetical, which were written out above, four of them make the consequence on the supposition that the term a is; while four propose the condition that the term a is not. Syllogisms come from them in this way. From the first proposition: if a is, when b is, c is; but a is; therefore when b is, c is. Or thus: but when b is, c is not; therefore a is not. That such an assumption is possible is known from the nature of the propositions described above. From the second proposition: if a is, when b is, c is not; but a is; therefore when b is, c is not. Or thus: but when b is, c is; therefore a is not. From the third: if a is, when b is not, c is; but a is; therefore when b is not, c [is]. Or thus: but when b is not, c is not; therefore a is not. From the fourth: if a is, when b is not, c is not; but a is; therefore when b is not, c [is not]. Or thus: but when b is not, c is; therefore a is not. In these four propositions, then, in which the term a is proposed to be, if it is assumed that this same term a is, the term c is shown either to be or not to be. But if the term c is assumed — that is, if it is assumed not to be when it is [proposed to be], or to be when it is [proposed] not [to be] — the term a will be shown not to be. From the fifth proposition the syllogisms come about thus: if a is not, when b is, c is; but a is not; therefore when b is, c is. Or thus: but a is; therefore when b is, c is not. Or thus: but when b is, c is not; therefore a is. Or thus: but when b is, c is; therefore a [is] not. The reason why a proposition of this kind gathers four syllogisms is that 'if something is not, another is' can be proposed only in cases where contraries lack intermediates; for in these, either when one is destroyed the other is posited, or when one is posited the other must be removed. From the sixth: if a is not, when b is, c is not; but a is not; therefore when b is, c is not. Or thus: but when b is, c is; therefore a is. From the seventh: if a is not, when b is not, c is; but a is not; therefore when b is not, c is. Or thus: but a is; therefore when b is not, c is not. Or thus: but when b is not, c is not; therefore a is. Or thus: but when b is not, c is; therefore a is not. In this combination too, for the same reason, four inferences come about. From the eighth: if a is not, when b [is not], c is not; but a is not; therefore when b is not, c is not. Or thus: but when b is not, c is; therefore a is. In these four propositions too, if it is assumed that a is not, the term c is concluded either to be or not to be. But if c is assumed not to be when it is [proposed to be], or to be when it is [proposed] not [to be], the term a is always concluded to be, except only in the fifth and seventh modes, where, when c is assumed to be, a is shown not to be. For all of them there is a common rule, except the fifth and seventh modes: if the term a is assumed in the way in which it was proposed in the first statement, the condition which follows is confirmed in the conclusion. But if the condition which follows is assumed in the contrary way to that in which it was proposed in the statement, the categorical proposition, which comes first, is destroyed. In the seventh or fifth mode, however, either one, assumed in either way, will produce a conclusion in both parts. And so there come to be sixteen, or rather twenty, syllogisms: eight if the term a is assumed as it was proposed, and eight if the term c is assumed in the converse way to that in which it was posited in the proposition; and four from the seventh and fifth modes, which produce a conclusion either way. In the remaining combinations there is no consequence of necessity.
