So that the understanding might be plainer, I have noted down the propositions themselves set out with their terms, so that according to the modes of assumption stated above, not only would a demonstration be made by reasoning, but the teaching would also shine out more clearly to those running through it by way of example.
If a is man, when b is animate, c is animal.
If a is man, when b is animate, c is not insentient.
If a is man, when b is not animate, c is sentient.
If a is man, when b is not animate, c is not insentient.
If a is not animate, when b is insentient, c is lifeless.
If a is not animate, when b is insentient, c is not alive.
If a is not animate, when b is not sentient, c is lifeless.
If a is not animate, when b is not sentient, c is not living.

Now that we have set out these syllogisms which come from propositions of the kind that are coupled with a predicative first and a hypothetical second, let us now pass to those which are joined from a conditional first and a predicative second. The number of all of these must be set down, so that the reader may know what we are speaking about.
If, when a is, b is, c is.
If, when a is, b is, c is not.
If, when a is, b is not, c is.
If, when a is, b is not, c is not.
If, when a is not, b is, c is.
If, when a is not, b is, c is not.
If, when a is not, b is not, c is.
If, when a is not, b is not, c [is] not.

The first proposition, then, must have terms such that a can be apart from b and c; but then, if a is, c must be, when the term b follows the term a. For example, let a be animate, b man, c animal: for the animate can be both apart from man and apart from animal. But then what is animate must be an animal, if what is animate is a man. The second proposition is to be woven from terms such that a can be both apart from b and c and together with them; yet c must then not be when b is, if b follows when a is posited. For example, let a be animate, b man, c horse. For it can come about that the animate is a man, or a horse. But then what is animate must not be a horse, if that very thing which is animate is a man. The third proposition is coupled from these terms: a can either be or not be with b and c, yet it must then be together with c, if, when the term a is posited, the term b is denied. For example, let a be animal, b animal, c insentient. For what is animate can be either animal or not animal, and either insentient or not insentient; but then what is animate must be insentient, if, when animate is posited, animal is denied. The terms of the fourth proposition are these: a can both be and not be with b and with c, but then c is separated from it in every way, if, when the term a is posited, the term b is denied. For example, let a be animate, b animal, c man. For what is animate can both be and not be an animal, and likewise both be and not be a man; yet it is then necessary that, when it is animate, it is not a man, when, animate being posited, it is denied to be an animal. The fifth proposition is connected from these terms: if a is not, b and c can both be and not be; yet then, when a is not, the term c must be, if, when a is posited not to be, it follows that the term b is. For example, let a be lifeless, b man, c animal. For if it is not lifeless, then man and animal can either be or not be; but then it is necessary for it to be an animal when lifeless is denied, if, when lifeless is denied, it follows that it is a man. The sixth proposition should be joined by such members that, if the term a is not, b and c can either be or not be; but then, when the term a is denied, c must not be, when the affirmation of the term b accompanies the negation of the term a. For example, let a be lifeless, b man, c horse. For what is not lifeless can either be or not be a man or a horse; but it is necessary that it is not a horse when lifeless is denied, if the positing of man follows the negation of lifeless. The terms of the seventh proposition will have to be these: if a is not, the terms b and c can both be and not be; but then the term c must be, if the negation of the term b follows the negation of the term a. For example, let a be animal, b animate, c lifeless: if it is not an animal, it can both be and not be animate and lifeless. But then it is necessary, if it is not an animal, that it is lifeless, when, if it is not an animal, it will not be animate. The eighth proposition is when, the term a being denied, the terms b and c can both be and not be. But then it is necessary, if the term a is denied, that the term c is not, when the negation of the term b follows the negation of the term a. For example, let a be lifeless, b animal, c man. If, then, it is not lifeless, it can both be and not be an animal and a man. These matters being thus set out, this must be said in common: that the first four propositions make the condition on the supposition that a is, and the latter four on the supposition that it is not; and from all of them syllogisms arise in this way. From the first proposition: if, when a is, b is, c is; but, when a is, b is; therefore c is. Or thus: but c is not; therefore, when a is, b is not. That such conclusions can come about we recognise from the nature of the propositions described above: for the term a could both be and not be with b. Likewise from the second: if, when a is, b is, c is not; but, when a is, b is; therefore c is not. Or thus: but c is; therefore, when a is, b is not. From the third, however, inferences come about with the terms assumed either way: as, if, when a is, b is not, c is; but, when a is, b is not; therefore c is. Or thus: but, when a is, b is; therefore c is not. Or thus: but c is not; therefore, when a is, b is. Or so: but c is; therefore, when a is, b is not. The inference came about either way for this reason: because these propositions could be posited in terms in which immediate contraries were found. For in those, the positing of one destroyed the other, and the removal of one posited the other. From the fourth: if, when a is, b is not, c is not; but, when a is, b is not; therefore c is not. Or thus: but c is; therefore, when a is, b is. From the fifth: if, when a is not, b is, c is; but, when a is not, b is; therefore c is. Or so: but c is not; therefore, when a is not, b is not. From the sixth: if, when a is not, b is, c is not; but, when a is not, b is; therefore c is not. Or so: but c is; therefore, when a is not, b is not. From the seventh there is an inference either way, in this manner: if, when a is not, b is not, c is; but, when a is not, b is not; therefore c is. Or thus: but, when a is not, b is; therefore c is not. Or thus: but c is not; therefore, when a is not, b is. Or so: but c is; therefore, when a is not, b is not. Here too, for the same reason, a syllogism will come about in either assumption; for it was said that something is when another is not only in immediate contraries. From the eighth: if, when a is not, b is not, c is not; but, when a is not, b is not; therefore c is not. Or thus: but c is; therefore, when a is not, b is. In all the syllogisms described above, then, the rule is this: if the term b is assumed as it was posited in the proposition, it concludes the term c as it had been placed in the same proposition. But if the term c is assumed in the contrary way to that in which it was posited in the proposition, the term b will be shown in the conclusion in the contrary way, except in the third and seventh modes, in which, even if the term b is assumed in the contrary way to that in which it was posited in the proposition, it infers the term c in the contrary way to that in which it was posited; or, if the term c is assumed as it was posited in the proposition, it concludes the term b in like manner as it had been placed in the same proposition. Therefore there come to be sixteen, or rather twenty, syllogisms: for when the first, hypothetical, propositions are assumed, there are eight; and eight if the second, predicative, ones are assumed; and to these are added four from the third and seventh modes, which infer either way, so that in these combinations of propositions too there come to be in all sixteen or twenty syllogisms. But in whatever other way you turn the assumptions, nothing necessary results. So that the whole account of the propositions and syllogisms may shine out, we have added examples, by which what we taught above may become clear more easily: if, when a, animate, is, b, man, is, c, animal [is]; if, when a, animate, is, b, man [is], c, horse, is not; if, when a, animate, is not, b, animal, is, c, insentient [is]; if, when a, animate, is not, b, animal, is not, c, man [is not]; if, when a, lifeless, is not, b, man, is, c, animal, is; if, when a, lifeless, is not, b, man, is, c, horse, is not; if, when a, animal, is not, b, animate [is not], c, lifeless, is; if, when a, lifeless, is not, b, animal, is not, c, man, is not. And enough has been said about these syllogisms which are connected from such propositions as consist of a hypothetical and a predicative. Now we must speak of those syllogisms whose propositions are contained in three terms in such a way that they are intermediate between those which are woven from a hypothetical and a predicative and those which are connected from two hypotheticals. We set them out at this point because, like the preceding ones, these too are contained in three terms, and treatment proceeding from like to like will be easier. The syllogisms of these are manifold, and none of them can be perfect, since they are not evident in themselves and, for belief to be given to them, they need the help of a proof set from outside. The proof of such syllogisms is a syllogism constructed in another order; and they come about, as has been said, now through the first, now through the second, and now through the third figure. The propositions of the first figure are these:
If a is, b is, and if b is, c is.
If a is, b is, and if b is, c is not.
If a is, b is not, and if b is not, c is.
If a is, b is not, and if b is not, c is not.
If a is not, b is, and if b is, c is.
If a is not, b is, and if b is, c is not.
If a is not, [b is not,] and if b is not, c is.

If a is not, b is not, and if b is not, c is not. So if the method of inference is such that the assumption posits and confirms what the first statement pronounces, sixteen combinations must come about, of which only eight preserve the necessity of the consequence, while the other eight seem to have nothing fit to produce belief. Again, if the assumption overturns what the first proposition posits, in this way too sixteen combinations must come about, of which a firm necessity holds eight, while an unreliable variability quite often holds the other eight. The syllogisms come about now in the first figure, now in the second, and now in the third. Let us therefore set out all the modes of the three figures, beginning from the first, so that nothing escapes us. The first mode of the first figure comes from the first proposition, when we propose thus: if a is, b is, and if b is, c must be. For then, if a is, c too must be. The demonstration of this is as follows: if a is, it follows that b is, for that is what the first proposition proposes, that if a is, b is; but if b is, c is, for that is what the second part of the proposition pronounces, that if b is, it necessarily follows that c [is]. With these granted, it comes about that when a is, c too must be. We call this syllogism imperfect, because it needed the testimony of a proof. The proof was this demonstration by syllogism, for in this way we confirm the necessity of the consequent. For when it was proposed thus: if a is, b is, and if b is, it is necessary that c is, and the assumption posited what the affirmation had laid down, that a is, and such a conclusion was said to follow that assumption, namely that c necessarily is, and this was not evident from the nature and property of the syllogism itself, a proof by syllogism was added in this way: if a is, b is; but if b is, c is; therefore if a is, it is necessary that c is. And it is clear that the same method must be expected in the remaining cases. And this combination is the one which assumes and posits what had been placed first in the proposition; but if someone, positing, assumes what followed, there is no necessity of syllogism, as when we say: if a is, b is, and if b is, c must be; but c is; it is not necessary that b is or is not; and since it is not necessary that b is or is not, it will not be necessary that a is or is not. An example such as this will confirm the same: if it is a man, it is an animal, and if it is an animal, it will be an animate body; but it is an animate body; it will not be necessary that it is an animal, and therefore not a man either. The second mode of the first figure is this, when we propose thus: if a is, b is, and if b is, c necessarily is not; but a is; therefore c is not. Its demonstration is as follows: if a is, b is, for the first condition showed this, namely that if a is, b is; and when b is, c necessarily is not. For the consequence displayed this, in which it was pronounced that if b were, it followed of necessity that c too was not; therefore if a is, [c] will not be. But if the assumption posits what the proposition laid down last, that is, that c is not, there is no syllogism. For if it is proposed about some thing thus: if it is a man, it is an animal, and if it is an animal, it is not a stone; but it is not a stone; it will not be necessary either that it is or that it is not an animal; in the same way, not a man either, for if it is not a stone, it can be wood, or the other things which are neither animals nor counted among men. The third mode of the first figure, when the assumption posits what the first proposition placed, takes its beginning from the third proposition, when we propose thus: if a is, b is not, and if b is not, c must be. For here again, if the term a is assumed, as it is placed in the first statement, it will be said thus: but a is; therefore c is. The proof is like the preceding ones: since a is, b is not, and since b is not, c is; therefore since a is, c is. But if the term c is assumed, nothing necessary will come about, as if we propose thus: if it is a man, it is not insentient; if it is not insentient, it is an animal; but it is an animal; it is not necessary that it is a man. The fourth mode is the one which takes its beginning from the fourth proposition, and is formed from such a proposition: if a is, b is not, and if b is not, c too is not; for here, if a is, c necessarily is not. The demonstration is the same as in the earlier modes. But if it is assumed that c is not, there will be no necessity of the combination, in this way. Come, let it be proposed: if it is a man, it is not irrational, and if it is not irrational, it is not inanimate; but it is not inanimate; it is not necessary that it is a man. The fifth mode descends from the fifth statement, whose first proposition is this: if a is not, b is, [and] if b is, c too must be; but a is not; therefore c must be. Here too the condition stated earlier produces the consequence of necessity; but if what c is be assumed, no necessity will result. For let the proposition be: if it is not irrational, it is rational, and if it is rational, it is an animal; and if we assume: but it is an animal, it will not be necessary either that it is or that it is not irrational. The sixth mode is the one which the sixth proposition makes: if a is not, b is, and if b is, c is not; but a is not; therefore c is not. The demonstration is like the preceding ones; but if c is assumed, in the same way there is no syllogism. For if the proposition is: if it is not animate, it is inanimate, and if it is inanimate, it is not sentient; if we assume: but it is not sentient, it will not be necessary either that it is or that it is not animate. The seventh mode is the one which is from the seventh proposition: if a is not, b is not, and if b is not, c must be; but a is not; therefore c must be. But if c is assumed, nothing necessary comes about, for if we propose: if it is not animate, it is not an animal, and if it is not an animal, it is insentient; and we assume: but it is insentient, it is not necessary either that it is or that it is not animate. The eighth mode is the one proposed thus: if a is not, b is not, and if b is not, c necessarily is not; but a is not; therefore c is not; but if c is assumed, there will be no necessity. Come, let us propose thus: if it is not animate, it is not an animal, and if it is not an animal, it necessarily is not sentient; but it is not sentient; it will not be necessary that it is not animate, as trees, plants, and whatever is quickened only by a living soul and not also by a sentient one. So in the first figure, from three terms, sixteen hypothetical combinations come about, such that what is posited in the proposition is posited in the assumption too: eight if the term a is posited in the assumption, and eight if c. And if the term a is assumed by positing, there will be eight necessary syllogisms; but if the term c is assumed by positing, no syllogism is produced. In the same way too the order of syllogisms and combinations will be established if what had been posited in the proposition is removed in the assumption. For sixteen combinations will come about, of which the eight where what follows is removed continue with necessity intact, while the eight in which what precedes is removed [do not] preserve necessity in the same way. Let examples of all of these be appended. The first mode, then, is this: if a is, b is, and if b is, c too must be; but c is not; therefore a is not. But if we assume: but a is not, nothing necessary will result. For let this be the proposition: if it is a man, it is an animal, and if it is an animal, it must be animate; but it is not a man; therefore it will not be necessary that it is or is not animate. The second mode is: if a is, b is, and if b is, c necessarily is not; but c is; therefore a will not be. But if we assume thus: but a is not, it will not be necessary that c is or is not; for if the proposition is such: if it is a man, it is an animal, and if it is an animal, it is not a stone, if we assume: but it is not a man, it will not be necessary that it is or is not a stone. The third mode is: if a is, b is not, and if b is not, c must be; but c is not; therefore a necessarily is not. But if the assumption removes the term a, nothing necessary results. Come, let the proposition be: if it is a man, it is not inanimate, and if it is not inanimate, it must be animate; but it is not a man; it is not necessary that it is or is not animate. The fourth mode: if a is, b is not, and if b is not, c necessarily is not; but c is; therefore a will not be. But if we assume that a is not, no necessity of the combination is found; for if the proposition is: if it is a man, it is not irrational, [and] if it is not irrational, it necessarily is not inanimate; but it is not a man; it is not necessary that it is or is not inanimate. The fifth: if a is not, b is, and if b is, c too must be; but c is not; therefore a must be. But if the term a is assumed, no syllogism will come about; for let the proposition be: if it is not irrational, it is rational, and if it is rational, it is an animal; but it is irrational; it will not be necessary that it is or is not an animal. The sixth: if a is not, b is, and if b is, c necessarily is not; but c is; therefore a must be. But if I take the term a, no necessity is found; for let the proposition be such: if it is not animate, it is inanimate, and if it is inanimate, it is not sentient; but it is animate; it will not be necessary either that it is or that it is not sentient. The seventh: if a is not, b is not, and if b is not, c must be; but c is not; therefore a must be. But if we take the term a, the combination will produce no necessity; for let the proposition be such: if it is not an animal, it is not rational, [and] if it is not rational, it is irrational; and let us assume: but it is an animal; it is not necessary either that it is irrational or that it is not. The eighth mode is the one formed by this proposition: if a is not, b is not, and if b is not, c necessarily is not; but c is; therefore a must be. But if you take the term a, no necessity will come about; for let the proposition be: if it is not an animal, it is not a man, and if it is not a man, it necessarily is not capable of laughter; but it is an animal; it will not be necessary that it is or is not capable of laughter. And enough has been said about the first figure; the second will be treated in the following book.
BOOK TWO.

Of conditional propositions which consist of three terms, the second figure occurs whenever, when something is said [to be], it follows that two certain [things] are said either to be or not to be. They vary, moreover, in the propositions themselves and also in the conclusions, according to the order of the assumption, in many ways. So that this may become known more easily, let all the propositions first be set out in order. About them it must be said beforehand that the propositions are often posited in the same mode, but often not. About those in the same mode there is no syllogism. A proposition is in the same mode if we speak thus: if a is, b is, and if a is, c is not. But if they are in unlike modes, they make a syllogism. A proposition of the second figure that is not in the same mode is found in those hypothetical syllogisms whose statements are composed of three terms, as when we propose thus: if a is, b is, but if a is not, c is. Let an example of this proposition be understood as follows: if it is an animal, it is animate; if it is not an animal, it is insentient. Here, then, 'animal', which is a, is not proposed in one mode in both, but is joined affirmatively to b and negatively to c, and this is called being predicated not in the same mode. But if in both a were posited as being, or as not being, it would be called predication in the same mode. Let all the propositions not in the same mode, then, be set out (as has been said) in this way: if a is, b is, if a is not, c is; if a is, b is, if a is not, c is not; if a is, b is not, if a is not, c is; if a is, b is not, if a is not, c is not. Now, then, a's being has been posited with b, and its not being with c. Again let us posit a's not being with b, and its being with c: if a is not, b is, if a is, c is; if a is not, b is, if a is, c is not; if a is not, b is not, if a is, c is; if a is not, b is not, if a is, c is not. If, then, the proposition is not in the same mode, when b is assumed sixteen combinations come about, of which only eight are syllogisms. Again, if c is assumed, sixteen combinations likewise come about, but in only eight is the firm necessity of syllogisms found. Let, then, the first mode of the second figure be this one, coming from the first proposition: if a is, b is, but if a is not, c is. I say that if b is not, c is. For since if a is, b is, according to the order of consequence, if b is not, a will not be; but if a were not, c would be; if, then, b is not, c will be. But if that same b is posited as being, nothing necessary results. For come, let b be: it is not necessary either that a is or that it is not. Nothing necessary follows, then, so that c either is or is not; as if a is animal, b animate, c insentient: for if it is an animal, it is animate; but if it is not an animal, it is insentient; but if it is animate, it is not necessary that it is an animal, or that it is not; it is therefore not necessary that it is insentient, or that it is not. But if the term c is assumed, then if it is posited as not being, b will necessarily be; but if as being, there will be no syllogism. For if c is not, a is; but if a is, b is; if, then, c is not, b is. But if c is, it is not necessary that a is, or perhaps it may be necessary that it is not. For this proposition, likewise: if a is not, c is, occurs only in such [terms] of which one or the other must be. But if c is, a will not be; [and] if a is not, [this has] nothing to do with b; as, if it is insentient, it will not be an animal, but if it is not an animal, it will not be necessary that it is or is not animate at all. Again, a syllogism comes from the second proposition when we propose thus: if a is, b is, if a is not, c is not. I say that if b is not, c is not. For it was proposed: if a is, b is; and the order of consequence is: if b is not, a is not; but if a is not, c is not; if, then, b is not, c is not. But if b is, it is not necessary that c is. For let a be animal, b animate, c rational, and let it be proposed: if it is an animal, it is animate, if it is not an animal, it is not rational; but if it is animate, it is not necessary that it is an animal, with the result that [it is not necessary that it is] rational either. But if the assumption names the term c, then if the term c is affirmed, b will be; but if that same term c is denied, there is no syllogism. For since if a is, b will be, [and] if a is not, c will not be, if c is, a will be; but when a is, b is; if, then, c [is], b will be. But if c is not, nothing is necessary. For in this proposition which says: if it is an animal, it is animate, if it is not an animal, it is not rational, let us assume: but it is not rational; it will not be necessary that it is or is not an animal, and therefore not [that it is or is not] animate either. Likewise from the third proposition the syllogism is such: if a is, b is not, and if a is not, c is. I say that if b is, c is. For since it has been proposed thus: if a is, b is not, it must follow that if b is, a is not; but if a is not, c will be; if, then, b is, c will be. But if b is not, nothing is necessary. For let a be animal, b inanimate, c insentient: in this proposition which says: if it is an animal, it is not inanimate, if it is not an animal, it is insentient, if we assume: it is not inanimate, it will not be necessary that it is or is not an animal, and therefore not [that it is or is not] insentient either. But if the assumption is made from the term c, then if c is not, b will not be; but if c is, there will be no necessity of conclusion. For since it has been proposed thus, that if a is, b is not, but if a is not, c [is], the consequence of things is such that if c is not, a is; for this can be said only in terms which lack an intermediate. But if a is, b is not. If, then, c is not, b will not be. But if c is, there is no syllogism. For in this proposition which says: if it is an animal, it is not inanimate, but if it is not an animal, it is insentient, let someone assume that it is insentient; it follows indeed that it is not an animal, but it does not follow that it either is or is not animate. From the fourth proposition there is a syllogism thus: if a is, b is not, if a is not, c is not. I say that if b is, c is not. For since it has been proposed thus: if a is, b is not, the consequence of things is such that if b is, a is not; but when a is not, it had been posited that c is not. If, then, b is, c is not. But if b is assumed not to be, there will be no syllogism. For come, let a be animal, b inanimate, c rational, and let this be the proposition: if it is an animal, it is not inanimate, if it is not an animal, it is not rational; let us then assume that it is not inanimate: it will not be necessary that it is an animal, and therefore not [that it is] rational either. Again, if the term c is assumed, then if it is posited as being, it will be necessary that b is not. But if c is not, there is no syllogism. For since it was proposed that if a is, b is not, [and] if a is not, c is not, it is necessary that when c is, a also is; but if a is, b is not; if, then, c is, b will not be. But if c is posited as not being, there is no syllogism, as in this proposition: if it is an animal, it is not inanimate, if it is not an animal, it is not rational. If, then, someone assumes that it is not rational, it will not be necessary that it is or is not an animal, and therefore not [necessary] that it is or is not inanimate either. And in these four propositions the term a has been so posited that with b it was said to be, and with c not to be. But if the order is changed, there will again be four other syllogisms if the term b is assumed, and four others also if c; and on each side there will be four combinations which make no syllogisms. For let the fifth proposition be: if a is not, b is, if a is, c is. I say that if b is not, c will be. For let it be assumed: but b is not; a will therefore be, for this was established to be the method of consequence. But when a is, c is; if, then, b is not, c will be. But if b is posited as being, nothing is necessary; for if b is, a will not be; but if a is not, [this has] nothing to do with c; therefore there is no syllogism. That a is not, if b is, is shown by the proposition by which we say: if a is not, b is. For this occurs only in immediate contraries. For come, let a be animal, b insentient, and c animate, and let it be proposed: if it is not an animal, it is insentient, if it is an animal, it is animate; and let it be posited that it is insentient: it is necessary that it is not an animal. But it is not necessary that it either is or is not animate. But if the term c is assumed, then [if assumed] negatively it will make a syllogism, but affirmatively in no way. For if c is not, a is not. But if a is not, b is; if, then, c [is not], b is. But if c is, it is not necessary that a is or is not, with the result that it is not necessary that b is or is not either. For if it is animate, it is not necessary that it is or is not an animal; and when it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it either is or is not insentient. The proposition is the same as in the preceding. Again, from the sixth proposition a syllogism comes about in this way: if a is not, b is, and if a is, c is not. I say that if b is not, c will not be. For if b is not, a is; but if a is, c is not; if, then, b is not, c will not be. But if the assumption posits the term b, there is no necessity of conclusion. For if b is, a is not (this is clear from the preceding); but if a is not, [this has] nothing to do with c, for c was not [only] if a were. The example is this: let a be animal, b insentient, c inanimate. If, then, the proposition is such: if it is not an animal, it is insentient, if it is an animal, it is not inanimate. But it is insentient; it is therefore not an animal; but it does not follow that it is or is not inanimate. But if we take the term c, then if you affirm [it], you will make a syllogism; for if c is, a will not be; but if a is not, b will be. If, then, c is, b will be. But if you deny c, nothing is necessary. For if we assume: but c is not, it will not be necessary that a is or is not, and therefore not b either. For if you deny 'inanimate', it is not necessary that it is or is not an animal, and therefore not [necessary] that it is or is not insentient either. From the seventh proposition there is a conclusion when we propose thus: if a is not, b is not, if a is, c is. I say that if b is, c will be. For since it has been proposed thus, that if a were not, b would not be, a will be if b is. But if a is, c will be. If, then, b is, c will be. But if the assumption denies the term b, there will be no necessity in the conclusion. For if b is not, it will not be necessary at all that a is or is not, and therefore not c either; as in these terms: let a be animate, b animal, c living. If we state thus: if it is not animate, it is not an animal, if it is animate, it lives; if, then, we assume: but it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it is or is not animate, and therefore not [necessary that it] lives either. But if we assume the term c, then if we deny [it], there will be the perfect necessity of a syllogism; but if we affirm [it], there is no conclusion. For if c is not, a will not be; [and] if a is not, b will not be; if, then, c is not, b will not be. But if c is affirmed, nothing is necessary; for whether it is necessary that a is, or not necessary that a is, [this has] nothing to do with b, as can be shown in the preceding terms. For if it lives, even if it is necessary that it is animate, it is not on that account necessary that it is an animal or that it is not; and if it is not necessary that it is animate, it is not necessary that it is or is not an animal; but that it should be necessary that it is not animate cannot happen. From the eighth proposition the conclusion is such, when it is proposed thus: if a is not, b is not, and if a [is], c is not. I say that if b is, c is not; for if b is, a is; but if a is, c is not; if, then, b is, c will not be; But if the assumption denies the term b, nothing is necessary. For if b is not, it will not be necessary that a is or is not, and so it follows that c is not [necessary] either, as in these terms: let a be animate, b animal, c inanimate. If, then, we propose: if it is not animate, it is not an animal; if it is animate, it is not inanimate; and we assume: but it is not an animal; it is not necessary that it is or is not animate, and therefore not [that it is or is not] inanimate either. But if the term c is assumed, then if it is posited with an affirmation, there will be the necessity of a syllogism. For if c is, a is not; and if a is not, b is not; if, then, c is, b is not. But if the assumption denies the term c, nothing is necessary. For if c is not, it will not be necessary that a is or is not, and so it follows that b is not [necessary] either. For if it is not inanimate, perhaps it is indeed necessary that it is animate, but it is not necessary that it is an animal. Terms will also be found in which it is not necessary that a is, as if we posit c as black and a as white: it does not follow from the negation of black that white is affirmed. And we have now, I think, set out all the combinations of the second figure that are not in the same mode; but if they are in the same mode, no syllogism at all comes about. They are in the same mode in this way: whenever the term a is posited as being, or as not being, with both b and c alike, in whatever way the terms b and c are varied. Of these combinations, then, which are said to be in the same mode, none can be combined [into a syllogism]. All the combinations in the same mode are these:
If a is, b is; if a is, c is. If a is, b is; if a is, c is not.
If a is, b is not; if a is, c is. If a is, b is not; if a is, c is not.
If a is not, b is; if a is not, c is. If a is not, b is.
If a is not, c is not. If a is not, b is not; if a is not, c is.
If a is not, b is not; if a is not, c is not.

Let us find that their conclusion is weak and wholly lacking in necessity, from assumptions made in whatever way; and also, following the modes described above, we shall very easily be able to find terms by which it may be shown that no constancy can be found in such combinations. And so we have shown carefully, concerning the second figure, how many syllogisms there are and in how many modes they come about. If the combinations are not in the same mode, eight syllogisms come about when the term b is assumed, and as many if the term c is assumed; so there are sixteen syllogisms of the second figure, and as many combinations come about, when the terms b and c are not assumed as they should be, from which nothing at all is inferred. Now, then, we must speak of the third figure. In it as many combinations and as many syllogisms come about, but on condition that the propositions posited are not in the same mode; and if they are in the same mode, no syllogism at all will come about (as was said in the second figure). Let us, then, set out all [the combinations] of the third figure in propositions not in the same mode: if b is, a is; if c is, a is not. If b is, a is; if c is not, a is not. If b is not, a is; if c is, a is not. If b is not, a is; if c is not, a is not. And here a has been proposed as being with b, but as not being with c. Again, let a be proposed as not being with b, but as being with c: if b is, a is not; if c is, a is. If b is, a is not; if c is not, a is. If b is not, a is not; if c is, a is. If b is not, a is not; if c is not, a is not. The first mode of the third figure, then, is of this kind: if b is, a is; if c is, a is not. This differs from the first mode of the second figure. For there, if a was or was not, b and c were said to be; but now, if b or c are, a is proposed as either being or not being. Propositions are not in the same mode which lay down in one part that a is, in the other that a is not, as in the proposition given above: for if b is, a is; if c is, a is not. These things being so posited, I say that if b is, it is necessary that c is not. For if b is, a is; and if a is, c is not; if, then, b is, c is not. But if the term b is denied, there is no syllogism; for if b is not, it will not be necessary that a is or is not. Nor, then, will it be necessary that c either is or is not, as in this example: let b be animal, a animate, c dead, and let it be proposed: if it is an animal, it is animate; if it is dead, it is not animate. But [if] it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it is or is not animate. For things which are not animals can be animate, like trees; they can be not animate, like stones. Therefore, if it is not an animal, it is not necessary either that it is or is not dead. For many things are not animals which are not dead, like stones; for those things are called dead which once lived. But from the assumption of the term c, the affirmation will make a syllogism. For if c is, b will not be; for if c is, a is not; and if a is not, b will not be; if, then, c is, b will not be. But the negation of c sets out no necessity. For if c is not, it is not necessary that a is or is not, and so it follows that b is not [necessary] either. For if it is not dead, it is not necessary that it is animate or is not. For some things which are not dead are animate, like trees; but some, although they are not dead, are not animate, like stones; so it comes about [that] dead is removed. From the second proposition, the mode of inferring is this: if b is, a is; if c is not, a is not. I say that if b is, c will be. For if b is, a is; and if a is, c is. For such a proposition, which says: if c is not, a is not, is converted thus: if, then, [a] is, c is. But if the term b is denied, no necessity of syllogism comes about. For if b is not, it is not necessary that a is or is not. Therefore no necessity will reach c either, as is clear in these terms: let b be animal, a animate, c corporeal; and let it be proposed: if it is an animal, it is animate; if it is not corporeal, it is not animate; and let it be assumed: but it is not an animal; it is not necessary that it is or is not corporeal. But the term c, if it is denied, there will be the necessity of a syllogism. For if c is not, a is not; and if a is not, b is not, for it can be converted thus. If, then, c is not, b will not be. If c is affirmed, there is no necessity; for if it is corporeal, it is not necessary that it is animate or is not. Therefore it is not necessary either that it is or is not an animal. The third proposition admits such a conclusion: if b is not, a is; if c is, a is not. I say that if b is not, c will not be. For if b is not, a is; and if a is, c will not be; for that part of the proposition which said that if the term c is, the term a is not, could be converted thus. So it comes about that if b is not, c is not. But if they affirm that the term b is, there is no necessity of conclusion. For if b is, it is indeed necessary that a is not, but it is not necessary that c is, as in these terms: let b be animate, a [in]animate, c animal. If someone, then, proposes thus: if it is not animate, it is inanimate; if it is an animal, it is not inanimate. If, then, we posit that it is animate, it follows indeed that it is not inanimate, but it is not necessary that it is an animal. But if the term c is affirmed, a necessary conclusion will come about in this way. For if c is, a is not; if a is not, b is. For that followed the proposition which said that if the term b was not, the term a was. If, then, c is, b is. But if the same term c is denied, there is no syllogism. For if c is not, it is not necessary that a is or is not, and so it follows that b is not [necessary] either. For if it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it is or is not inanimate; therefore not [that it is or is not] animate either. From the fourth proposition the syllogism is such: if b is not, a is; if c is not, a is not. I say that if b is not, c is. For if b is not, a is; and if a is, it is necessary that c is. For that follows the part of the proposition which says: if c is not, a is not. If, then, b is not, c is. But if the term b is affirmed, there is no syllogism. For it follows that a is not, but it does not follow that c is or is not, as in these terms. For if b is insentient, a animal, c animate, and it is proposed: if it is not insentient, it is an animal; if it is not animate, it is not an animal; [then] if it is insentient, it is not an animal, but it is not necessary that it is or is not animate. But if the term c is denied, a syllogism will come about at once. For if c is not, a is not; if a is not, b will be. For that follows the part of the proposition which says: if c is not, a is. If, then, c is not, b will be. But if c is, it is not necessary that a is or is not, and so it follows that b is not [necessary] either. For if it is animate, it is not necessary that it is an animal or is not, and so it follows that it is not necessary either that it is or is not insentient. And so far we have arranged four modes in such a way that the term a was posited as being in relation to the term b, however that term stood, and as not being in relation to c. Now let us set them out so that the term a is said not to be in relation to the term b, and to be in relation to c, the order, that is, being reversed. That all the propositions are not in the same mode is shown by the fact that a is proposed affirmatively in relation to b and negatively in relation to c, or, if negatively in relation to b, it keeps an affirmative statement in relation to c. The fifth proposition, then, makes the following syllogism, when the proposition is this: if b is, a is not; if c is, a is. I say that if b is, c is not. For if b is, a is not. And if a is not, c is not. For that followed the proposition which said that if the term c was, a also was. If, then, b is, c is not. But if b is denied, there is no syllogism. For if b is not, it is not necessary that a is, and so it follows that no necessity reaches c either. And the same is clear in terms. For if b is dead, a animate, c animal, and the proposition is this: if it is dead, it is not animate; if it is an animal, it is animate; and we assume that it is not dead, it is not necessary that it is or is not animate, for both things that are still animate and things that never were are not dead. Therefore it does not follow that it is or is not an animal. For what is not dead can be an animal, like a living dog, and can not be one, like a stone. But if the term c is affirmed, there will be a perfect conclusion that [b] is not. For if c is, a is; and if a is, b will not be. For that follows the mode of the proposition set out above. If, then, c is, b will not be. But if c is denied, no necessity is brought to bear either on a or on b, as in these terms. For if it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it is or is not either animate or dead. The conclusion of the sixth proposition is this: if b is, a is not; if c is not, a is. I say that if b is, c will be. For if b is, a is not; if a is not, c will be. For such is the consequence in this part of the proposition. If, then, b is, c will be. But if the term b is denied, nothing necessary will come about. For if b is not, no necessity follows that the terms a or c either are present or are not present, as is clear in terms. For if b is dead, a animate, c inanimate, and it is proposed: if it is dead, it is not animate; if it is not inanimate, it is animate; [then] if it is not dead, it is not necessary that it is or is not animate, and therefore not [that it is or is not] inanimate either. But if the term c is assumed, provided it is put in the negative, a valid conclusion will come about that the term b is not. For since c is not, a is; and if a is, b is not. If, then, c is not, b will not be. But if the term c is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For if c is, although it is necessary that a is not, no necessity will reach the term b, as is also clear in terms. For if it is inanimate, it is necessary that it is not animate, but it is not necessary that it is dead. The syllogism of the seventh proposition is such. Let it be stated: if b is not, a is not; if c is, a is. I say that if b is not, c is not. For if b is not, a will not be; and if a is not, c will not be. For the same followed the proposition in which it was said that if the term c was, it followed that a also was. If, then, b is not, c will not be. But if b is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For if b is, it is not necessary that either a or c is or is not, as is clear in terms. For if b is animate, a animal, c sentient, and the proposition is: if it is not animate, it is not an animal; if it is sentient, it is an animal; if it is assumed that it is animate, it is necessary neither that it is an animal nor that it is sentient. But if the assumption is made through the term c, then if it is affirmed there will be a firm conclusion; if it is denied there is no syllogism. For if c is, a is; if a is, b will be. For that followed the proposition which says that if b is not, a is not. If, then, c is, b will be. But if the same term c is denied, nothing is necessary. For if c is not, no necessity binds either the term a or the term b; as, if it is not sentient, it is perhaps not an animal, but it is not necessary that it is animate. And terms will be found in which it is not even necessary that a is not. The eighth mode is that in which it is proposed thus: if b is not, a is not; and if c is not, a is. I say that if b is not, c is not. For if b is not, a will not be. And if a is not, c will be. For that followed the part of the proposition which said: if c is not, a is. If, then, b is not, c will be. But if the term b is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For if b is, it is necessary neither that the term a is nor that it is not, and so it follows that the same holds of c. This is made clear by such an example: if b is animate, a animal, c insentient, and it is proposed: if it is not animate, it is not an animal; if it is not insentient, it is an animal. If, then, we affirm the term b in the assumption and say, 'but it is animate', it is not necessary that it is or is not an animal or insentient. Therefore there is no syllogism. But if the term c is denied, a syllogism will come about at once. For if c is not, a is; and if a is, b will be. If, then, c is not, b will be. But if the term c is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For even if it is necessary that the term a is not, nothing necessary falls to the term b. This is shown by such an example: if it is insentient, it is not an animal; but if it is not an animal, it is not necessary that it is or is not animate. In propositions not in the same mode, then, whether the term b or the term c is assumed, eight syllogisms necessarily come about on either side. The remaining eight combinations on either side lack necessity. But if [the propositions] are in the same mode, there is no syllogism at all. They are called 'in the same mode' whenever the term a is proposed as either being or not being in relation to both. All propositions in the same mode are of this kind:
If b is, a is; if c is, a is.
If b is, a is; if c is not, a is.
If b is not, a is; if c is, a is.
If b is not, a is; if c is not, a is.
If b is, a is not; if c is, a is not.
If b is, a is not; if c is not, a is not.
If b is not, a is not; if c is, a is not.
If b is not, a is not; if c is not, a is not.

In these, running through them both by the consequence of the propositions set out above and by examples, we can recognise clearly and with constancy that no necessity at all arises in the syllogisms. Therefore, when the proposition is woven from three terms, sixteen syllogisms arise from the first figure, sixteen syllogisms from the second, and the same number are also inferred from the third, so that all the syllogisms from three terms are forty-eight. It remains now for us to speak of those syllogisms which are connected by two hypotheticals, whose consequence has a mode similar to that in the propositions which were made from two categorical and simple [propositions]. For in all of them, if we wish to establish something, we shall assume the first part of the whole proposition; but if something is to be destroyed in the conclusion, the second will be denied. But whether the first is denied or the latter affirmed, no necessity at all arises, except in the fifth, seventh, thirteenth and fifteenth propositions. In these it is not the nature of the combination but the property of the terms that produces the consequence, as we showed happens in those syllogisms which consist of propositions contained by two simple [propositions]. I have set out the propositions of all those which consist of two hypotheticals; when the reader has recognised their differences, he must go back to the examples of those which were joined from simple and categorical [propositions]. All the differences of the propositions which are coupled from two hypotheticals are of this kind:
If, when a is, b is, then when c is, d is.
If, when a is, b is, then when c is, d is not.
If, when a is, b is, then when c is not, d is.
If, when a is, b is, then when c is not, d is not.
If, when a is, b is not, then when c is, d is.
If, when a is, b is not, then when c is, d is not.
If, when a is, b is not, then when c is not, d is.
If, when a is, b is not, then when c is not, d is not.
If, when a is not, b is, then when c is, d is.
If, when a is not, b is, then when c is, d is not.
If, when a is not, b is, then when c is not, d is.
If, when a is not, b is not, then when c is, d is.
If, when a is not, b is not, then when c is, d is not.
If, when a is not, b is not, then when c is not, d is.
If, when a is not, b is not, then when c is not, d is not.

In these propositions too it must be observed that, since they are sixteen, eight are varied in such a way that in all of them the term a is posited to be, and eight in such a way that the same term a is said not to be. But they will not have the force of conditional propositions consisting of two hypotheticals however they are set out. For if someone were to say thus: if, when it is a man, it is an animal, then when it is animate, it is a body, he has not made the proposition which consists of two conditionals. For it is not because what is a man is an animal that what is animate is a body, nor does condition follow condition; but if you separate them and pronounce them each by itself, each has necessity in the consequence of its terms. For both what is a man is an animal, and what is animate is a body, and these propositions are true by themselves, and are not joined by a condition. So that the nature of each may become clear, each one must be discussed. The first proposition, then, must be such that, if a is posited, the term b does not immediately follow, and likewise if c is posited, the term d need not follow; but when the term a is posited, the term c must be, and when b is posited, the term d must be. For then it will come about that if, when a is posited, b is, then when c is posited, d necessarily follows; for instance, if the terms are a man, b doctor, c animate, d craftsman. For when man is posited it is not necessary that he be a doctor, and when it is animate it is not necessary that it be a craftsman. But if it is a man, it is necessary that it be animate, and if he is a doctor, it is necessary that he be a craftsman. With this posited, therefore, it will come about that if, when it is a man, he is a doctor, then when it is animate, it is a craftsman. The second proposition must be such that a and b, and likewise c and d, can be apart from each other, but a cannot be apart from c, while b and d cannot be at the same time. For then it will come about that if, when the term a is posited, b has followed, then when c is posited, d necessarily is not; for instance, if a is man, b black, c animate, d white. For man can both be and not be apart from black, and animate apart from white; but man cannot be apart from animate, nor can black be with white; and it comes about that if, when it is a man, he is black, then when it is animate, it is not white. Likewise the terms of the third proposition will have to be such that a can be apart from b, but c can be neither with a nor with d; therefore it comes about that if, when the term a is posited, b is, then when the term c is denied, d necessarily is; for instance, let a be animate, b doctor, c inanimate, d craftsman. For animate can be apart from doctor, but inanimate can be joined neither with animate nor with craftsman; therefore if, when it is animate, it is a doctor, then when it is not inanimate, it is a craftsman. The fourth proposition is to be woven from these terms: that a can either be or not be with the term b, and c with d; but that it is in no way possible for a to be with c, nor b with d. For then it comes about that if, when a is posited, b follows, then when c is denied, d is also denied; for instance, if a is man, b black, c inanimate, d white. Man can both be and not be apart from black, and inanimate apart from white; yet it is possible neither for man to be with inanimate nor black with white; but if, when it is a man, he is black, it follows that when it is not inanimate, it is not white. The members of the fifth proposition are these: that a can both be and not be apart from b, and c apart from d, but a cannot be apart from c, and b and d can never be at the same time, in such a way that if one is not, the other must be; for then it will come about that if, when a is posited, b is denied, then when c is posited, d follows; for instance, if a is man, b sick, c animate, d healthy. Man can both be and not be apart from sickness, and animate apart from health; but if it is a man, it must be animate, and if it is not sick, it must be healthy; so it will happen that if, when it is a man, he is not sick, then when it is animate, it is healthy. The sixth proposition requires these terms: that a can both be and not be apart from b, and c apart from d; but the same a cannot be apart from c, nor d apart from b. For then it will come about that if, when a is posited, b is not, then when c is posited, d is not; for instance, if a is man, b craftsman, c animate, d doctor. Man can both be and not be apart from craft, and animate apart from medicine, but neither can man be apart from animate, nor doctor apart from craft. Hence it happens that if, when it is a man, he is not a craftsman, then when it is animate, it is not a doctor. The terms of the seventh proposition are these: that a can be apart from b, but c can be neither with d nor with a, and b also cannot be at the same time with c; for so it comes about that if, when a is posited to be, b is denied, then when the term c is denied, d follows; for instance, if a is animate, b healthy, c inanimate, d sick. Animate can both be and not be apart from health, but inanimate can agree neither with animate nor with sick. Hence it happens that if, when it is animate, it is not healthy, then when it is not inanimate, it is sick. Likewise the eighth proposition is to be coupled with these terms: that a can both be and not be apart from the term b, but c can be neither with a nor with d, and d cannot be apart from b. For on this condition it will come about that if, when a is posited, b is denied, then when the term c is denied, the term d is not; for instance, if [a] is animate, b craftsman, c inanimate, d doctor. For animate can both be and not be apart from craft, but inanimate agrees neither with animate nor with doctor, and a doctor cannot be apart from craft; whence it comes about that if, when it is animate, it is not a craftsman, then when it is not inanimate, it is not a doctor. The ninth proposition will arise if a and b cannot be at the same time, while c can be apart from d but cannot be with a. For then it will come about that if, when a is denied, b follows to be, then when c is posited, d follows; for instance, if a is inanimate, b doctor, c animate, d craftsman. For what is inanimate cannot be a doctor, but what is animate can not be a craftsman, and inanimate and animate cannot be at the same time. Hence it happens that if, when it is not inanimate, it is a doctor, then when it is animate, it is a craftsman. Such terms will couple the tenth proposition: that a can be apart from b, and c apart from d, but a cannot be with c, nor b with d; for so it will turn out that if, when a is denied to be, b follows, then when the term c is posited, d necessarily is not; for instance, if a is inanimate, b black, c animate, d white. For inanimate can both be and not be apart from black, and animate apart from white. But inanimate and animate, and black and white, cannot be at the same time. But if inanimate is denied and black follows, then when animate is posited, white will be denied. Again, let the eleventh proposition be such that neither a with b, nor c with d, can be at the same time, while a cannot be without c, nor b without d. For so, if when a is denied b follows, then when c is denied, d necessarily is. For instance, if a is inanimate, b doctor, c lifeless, d craftsman: what is inanimate cannot be a doctor, and so what is lifeless cannot be a craftsman either; but what is inanimate cannot not be lifeless, and likewise whoever is a doctor cannot not be a craftsman. If therefore inanimate is denied and it follows that [the thing] is a doctor, then when it is denied to be lifeless, it follows that it is a craftsman. The twelfth proposition is one that will have to consist of terms such that a can either be or not be apart from b, and c apart from d, but a cannot be without c, nor b with d. For so it will fall out that if, when a is denied, b follows, then when c is denied, d is also denied. For instance, if a is inanimate, b white, c lifeless, d black: inanimate can either be or not be apart from white, and lifeless apart from black. Yet if a man is not inanimate and is white, then when he is not lifeless, he will not be black. The thirteenth proposition is to be connected by these terms: that a can be apart from b, and c apart from d, but a and c, and b and d, cannot be at the same time, in such a way that if one of them is not, the other necessarily is. For so it will happen that if, when a is denied, b is denied, then when c is affirmed, d is affirmed. For instance, if a is irrational, b sick, c rational, d healthy. For the irrational can be apart from the sick, and the rational apart from health, but irrational and rational, and sick and healthy, cannot be at the same time; yet if one of them is not, the other necessarily is. And so it happens that if, when irrational is denied, sick is denied, then when rational is posited, healthy is posited. The fourteenth proposition is to be woven from these members: that a can be apart from b, and c apart from d, but a and c cannot be at the same time, in such a way that when one is not, the other necessarily is; while d cannot be apart from b. It happens therefore that if, when a is denied, b is denied, then when c is, d is not. For instance, if a is inanimate, b craftsman, c animate, d doctor. The inanimate can be apart from a craftsman, and the animate apart from a doctor, but inanimate does not go together with animate, and a doctor is in no way separated from a craftsman. It happens therefore that if, when it is not inanimate, it is not a craftsman, then when it is animate, it is not a doctor. The fifteenth proposition ought to have these terms: that if a is not, c necessarily is not, while b and d are such that when one of them is denied, the other of them necessarily is. For so it will happen that if, when a is denied, b is denied, then when c is denied, d is affirmed. For instance, if a is irrational, b healthy, c inanimate, d sick: if [something] is not irrational, it is not inanimate; also healthy and sick cannot be at the same time, and whoever denies healthy must affirm sick, and likewise conversely. So it is the case that if, when irrational is denied, healthy is denied, then when inanimate is denied, sick is posited. The sixteenth proposition is the one that consists of these terms: that a cannot be apart from c, nor d apart from b, while a with b, and c with d, can in no way be. It comes about therefore that if, when a is denied, b is denied, then when c is denied, the term d is rejected. For instance, if a is inanimate, b craftsman, c lifeless, d doctor; the inanimate, then, cannot be apart from the lifeless, nor a doctor apart from a craftsman, but the inanimate cannot be with a craftsman, nor the lifeless with a doctor. If therefore, when inanimate is denied, craftsman is denied, then when lifeless is denied, doctor is denied. And this account of the propositions, whose examples we set out above, should be understood to have been adopted so that their nature might become clear, not because the terms could not be otherwise. For, as was said above, it is not enough to join terms in any way whatever for hypothetical propositions coupled from two conditionals to arise. For if someone says, 'If, when it is a man, it is an animal, then when it is day, it is light', he will not have made a proposition consisting of two conditions, because the first condition is not the cause of the second condition. This, then, is what the account of the propositions set out above demonstrates: how it comes about that condition follows condition. Since this is so, we must speak of their syllogisms. A syllogism arises, then, from the first proposition in this way: if, when a is, b is, then when c is, d is. But when a is, b is; therefore when c is, d will be. Or thus: but when c is, d is not; therefore when a is, b is not. That this assumption can be [made] is shown by the nature of the propositions described above. Likewise from the second proposition: if, when a is, b is, then when c is, d is not. But when a is, b is; therefore when c is, d is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is; therefore when a is, b is not. From the third: if, when a is, b is, then when c is not, d is. But when a is, b is; therefore when c is not, d is. Or thus: but when c is not, d is not; therefore when a is, b is not. Likewise from the fourth: if, when a is, b is, then when c is not, d is not. But when a is, b is; therefore when c is not, d is not. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is, b is not. From the fifth proposition four inferences arise, for the terms are so proposed that a valid conclusion arises either way, in this manner: if, when a is, b is not, then when c is, d is. But when a is, b is not; therefore when c is, d is. Or thus: but when a is, b is; therefore when c is, d is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is not; therefore when a is, b is. Or thus: but when c is, d is; therefore when a is, b is not. From the sixth: if, when a is, b is not, then when c is, d is not. But when a is, b is not; therefore when c is, d is not; or thus: but when c is, d is not [read: is]; therefore when a is, b is. Likewise from the seventh four syllogisms arise, in this manner: if, when a is, b is not, then when c is not, d is. But when a is, b is not; therefore when c is not, d is. Or thus: but when a is, b is; therefore when c is not, d is not. Or thus: but when c is not, d is not; therefore when a is, b is. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is, b is not. From the eighth proposition: if, when a is, b is not, then when c is not, d is not. But when a is, b is not; therefore when c is not, d is [read: is not]. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is, b is. So far, then, we have shown what syllogisms arise from propositions of this kind, which proposed that a is, and so varied the other terms by affirming and denying. Now we must say what syllogisms arise from those propositions which vary the other terms in such a way that they propose that a is not. From the ninth proposition a syllogism arises thus: if, when a is not, b is, then when c is, d is. But when a is not, b is; therefore when c is, d is. Or thus: but when c is, d is not; therefore when a is not, b is not. Likewise from the tenth: if, when a is not, b is, then when c is, d is not. But when a is not, b is; therefore when c [is], d is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is; therefore when a is not, b is not. From the eleventh: if, when a is not, b is, then when c is not, d is. But when a is not, b is; therefore when c is not, d is. Or thus: but when c is not, d is not; therefore when a is not, b is not. From the twelfth: if, when a is not, b is, then when c is not, d is not. But when a is not, b is; therefore when c is not, d is not. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is not, b is not. From the thirteenth, which infers four syllogisms in this manner: if, when a is not, b is not, then when c is, d is. But when a is not, b is not; [therefore] when c is, d is. Or thus: but when a is not, b is; therefore when c [is], d is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is; therefore when a is not, b is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is not; therefore when a is not, b is. Likewise from the fourteenth: if, when a is not, b is not, then when c is, d is not. But when a is not, b is not; therefore when c is, d is not. Or thus: but when c is, d is; therefore when a is not, b is. The fifteenth again infers four syllogisms, in this manner: if, when a is not, b is not, then when c is not, d is. But when a is not, b is not; therefore when c is not, d is. Or thus: but when a is not, b is; therefore when c is not, d is [read: is not]. Or thus: but when c is not, d is not; therefore when a is not, b is. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is not, b is not. From the sixteenth proposition: if, when a is not, b is not, then when c is not, d is not. But when a is not, b is not; therefore when c is not, d is not. Or thus: but when c is not, d is; therefore when a is not, b is. From all of these forty conclusions arise: sixteen with the first condition assumed as it is posited in the proposition, and sixteen with the second condition assumed in the contrary way to how it is placed in the proposition. Eight arise from the fifth, seventh, thirteenth and fifteenth propositions, with the first conditions assumed in the contrary way to how they were stated in the proposition, and the second conditions assumed in the same way as they had been placed in the proposition. So, in order that the account of all the propositions and conclusions may become clear, we have set out all statements of this kind with their own examples.
If, when a is a man, b is a doctor, then when c is animate, d is a craftsman.
If, when a is a man, b is black, then when c is animate, d is not white.
If, when a is animate, b is a doctor, then when c is not inanimate, d is a craftsman.
If, when a is a man, b is black, then when c is not inanimate, d is not white.
If, when a is a man, b is not sick, then when c is animate, d is healthy.
If, when a is a man, b is not a craftsman, then when c is animate, d is not a doctor.
If, when a is an animal, b is not healthy, then when c is not inanimate, d is sick.
If, when a is animate, b is not a craftsman, then when c is not inanimate, d is not a doctor.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is a doctor, then when c is animate, d is a craftsman.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is black, then when c is inanimate, d is not white.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is a doctor, then when c is not lifeless, d is a craftsman.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is white, then when c is lifeless, d is not black.
If, when a is not irrational, b is not sick, then when c is rational, d is healthy.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is not a craftsman, then when c is animate, d is not a doctor.
If, when a is not irrational, b is not healthy, then when c is not inanimate, d is sick.
If, when a is not inanimate, b is not a craftsman, then when c is not lifeless, d is not a doctor.

Let this, then, be what is said about those [syllogisms] that arise through connection. Those that are set in disjunction seem to be joined to them, and to take on the modes and forms of those which we said above, when set in connection, arise from propositions joined from two simple ones. If, therefore, I show that the propositions set out in disjunction correspond, by a likeness of their grounds, to those which, set in connection, are coupled from simple ones, then as many modes and whatever conclusions there are in each of those propositions that arise through connection, so many must there also be in these which, though stated through disjunction, are shown to have the same force as connection. We said above, then, that there are four differences of propositions stated through connection, if they are coupled from simple propositions, in this manner: if a is, b is; if a is not, b is not; if a is, b is not; if a is not, b is. Propositions through disjunction also hold four differences, in this manner: either a is, or b is; either a is not, or b is not; either a is, or b is not; either a is not, or b is. Of these, the first, which proposes "either a is, or b is", can be said only in those cases where one of the two must be, as in contraries lacking an intermediate, and it is like the proposition which says: if a is not, b is. For the one which proposes "either a is, or b is" means this: that both cannot be at once, and that if one is not, it follows that the other is. And so, if a is not, b will be; but this is one of the propositions which we enumerated above among those that arise through connection. Whatever syllogisms, therefore, arise in the proposition "if a is not, b is", these are also to be made in the one proposed through disjunction, as when we say "either a is, or b is". In the former, then, they arise in four modes. For whichever part of the proposition you assume, whether the antecedent or the consequent, whether in the negative or the affirmative mode, it will make a syllogism. For if the proposition is "if a is not, b is": if a is not, b will be; if a is, b will not be; if b is not, a will be; if b is, a will not be. In the disjunctive proposition too it is the same. For when it is said "either a is, or b is": if a is, b will not be; but if a is not, b will be; and if b is not, a will be; if b is, a will not be. This too is made clear by an example of this kind: if the proposition is "either he is sick, or he is healthy", whichever of these is assumed or denied in the assumption, the other part will be either affirmed or denied, in this manner: for if he is healthy, he is not sick; if he is not healthy, he is sick; if he is sick, he is not healthy; if he is not sick, he is healthy. Again, the disjunctive proposition which proposes "either a is not, or b is not" is made about things which in no way can be at once, even if it is not necessary that one of them be; and it is like the connected proposition by which it is proposed thus: if a is, b is not. For the one that states thus, "either a is not, or b is not", means precisely that if a is, b cannot be; and this will be proved thus: when it is proposed in this manner, "either a is not, or b is not", then if it is assumed that a is, b will not be. Hence it is like the connected proposition that states thus: if a is, b is not. In this proposition, however, only two combinations produced syllogisms. For if a was, b was not; and if b was, a was not. If a was not, it was not necessary for b either to be or not to be; and if b was not, it was not necessary for a either to be or not to be. Hence in the disjunctive proposition too there must be as many syllogisms, and as many combinations yielding no inference. For when it is proposed thus, "either a is not, or b is not", what is said is: if a is, b will not be; and if b is, a will not be. But if a is not, it will not be necessary for b either to be or not to be; and if b is not, it will not be necessary for a either to be or not to be, as appears in these examples. For if someone says "either it is not white, or it is not black", and assumes "but it is white", it will not be black; or again, "but it is black", it will not be white. But if he assumes that it is not white, it will not be necessary for it either to be or not to be black; and if he assumes that it is not black, [then] whether or not it is white, he will create no necessity. Again, the proposition by which it is proposed thus, "either a is, or b is not", is said of things that cleave to one another, and is proposed in those propositions which pass from greater to lesser; and it is like the connected proposition that states: if a is not, b is not. For if someone says "either a is, or b is not", and assumes "but a is not", b will by all means not be. So if a is not, b will not be; for this is what this disjunction put forward. In that [connected proposition], if a was denied or b affirmed, some syllogism arose; but if a was affirmed or b denied, there was no necessity in the conclusion. The same happens in the disjunctive. For when it is proposed "either a is, or b is not": if a is not, b will not be; if b is, a will be; but if a is, or b is not, nothing is necessary. We shall confirm this in these terms, if someone proposes thus: "either it is an animal, or it is not a man". If, then, it is not an animal, it will not be a man; if it is a man, it is an animal; but if it is an animal, it is not necessary that it be a man, and if it is not a man, it is not necessary that the animal perish. The proposition which says "either a is not, or b is" can be proposed in things that cleave together and pass from lesser to greater, and it is like the connected proposition that says: if a is, b is. For when someone states it thus, if it is assumed that a is, it at once follows that b is. But in that [connected] proposition, if it was affirmed that a is, it followed that b was; and if b was denied, it followed that a was not; but if a was denied or b affirmed, nothing necessary will be seen to result. So in the disjunctive proposition which says "either a is not, or b is", if a is, b will be; if b is not, a will not be; but if a is not, or b is, there is no necessity of syllogism, as is made clear in this example: "either it is not a man, or it is an animal". If, then, we assume "but it is a man", it will be an animal; if we deny that it is an animal, it will not be a man; but if we deny man, or affirm animal, nothing necessary will follow. Hence from what has been said above it is made clear how many syllogisms of disjunctive propositions there are, and by what differences they are separated from those that are connected. For connected ones show a certain consequence in being or not being, while those proposed through disjunction are such that they cannot agree with one another. You will also find propositions through connection which intend it to be understood that [their parts] cannot be separated from one another, as when we propose thus: if a is, b is. This proposition surely means that if a can be, it at once follows that b also is. But none of those in disjunction is proposed in such a way that they seem to be at once. For when we say "either a is, or b is", or vary the same propositions in any other way, the conjunction "either", which is set down as disjunctive, means that they cannot be at once. And since the difference between them extends widely, we have added a little about them now, because we were saying that as many syllogisms arise in propositions made through disjunction as there were also in connected ones. And since enough has been said about all the hypothetical syllogisms that can arise in any way, let us here bring the length of this work to an end.
